Clinical Reference

Opioid Overdose & Toxidromes

On this page
Opioid overdose is a breathing problem, not a consciousness problem: μ-receptor agonism silences the brainstem respiratory rhythm, producing the triad of depressed mental status + pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression. Ventilate first, then give naloxone — and titrate it to breathing, not to wakefulness.
Triad: coma · miosis · ↓RR Naloxone 0.4 mg IV/IM · 4 mg IN · repeat q2–3 min Infusion = ⅔ of the waking dose per hour Observe ≥1–2 h from the LAST naloxone dose ~70,400 US overdose deaths in 2025 (↓13.5%) Discharge = naloxone kit + MOUD handoff
Shared

Pathophysiology & classification

🧬

Mechanism — why opioids stop you breathing

Every opioid effect you will ever see — the analgesia people want, the euphoria that drives use, and the apnea that kills them — comes from one molecular event: an agonist occupying the μ-opioid receptor (MOR), a Gi/Go-coupled G-protein–coupled receptor. There are three classical opioid receptors (μ, κ, δ), but μ is the one that matters clinically: it delivers analgesia, euphoria, miosis, constipation, and — critically — respiratory depression. κ contributes dysphoria and some spinal analgesia; δ modulates mood. Drugs are dangerous in proportion to how hard and how fast they hit μ.

When an agonist binds MOR, the receptor splits its G-protein into two arms that both quiet the neuron:

  • Giα inhibits adenylyl cyclase → intracellular cyclic AMP falls → less PKA activity, less excitatory tone. (Chronic exposure drives the cell to upregulate adenylyl cyclase to compensate — this "cAMP overshoot" is the biochemical engine of withdrawal when the drug is removed.)
  • Gβγ opens GIRK potassium channels → K⁺ leaves the cell → the membrane hyperpolarizes → the neuron becomes much harder to fire.
  • Gβγ closes N-type voltage-gated calcium channels at the presynaptic terminal → less Ca²⁺ entry → less neurotransmitter release.

Now apply that to anatomy, because where the receptors sit explains the whole syndrome:

  • Pre-Bötzinger complex (ventrolateral medulla) — the pacemaker that generates the inspiratory rhythm. It is densely MOR-expressing. Silence it and the respiratory rate collapses; this is the primary killer.
  • Medullary and central chemoreceptors — normally, a rising PaCO₂ is the strongest stimulus to breathe. Opioids blunt the CO₂ response curve, so the patient does not feel air hunger even as CO₂ climbs. They quietly hypoventilate to death without ever struggling.
  • Edinger–Westphal nucleus (parasympathetic outflow to the pupil) — opioids disinhibit it, so parasympathetic tone to the iris sphincter goes unopposed → miosis.
  • Dorsal horn, periaqueductal grey, limbic system — analgesia, then sedation, then coma.
  • Gut myenteric plexus — slowed motility → constipation, decreased bowel sounds, and delayed absorption of co-ingestants.
Think of the pre-Bötzinger complex as a metronome that sets your breathing tempo, and CO₂ as the conductor who speeds it up when you fall behind. An opioid does two things at once: it slows the metronome and it puts headphones on the conductor. The tempo drifts to nothing, and nobody in the orchestra notices. Naloxone doesn't add a new instrument — it just pulls the earplugs out and takes the weights off the metronome by physically shoving the opioid off the receptor.
From receptor to arrest: one binding event, three signalling arms, and the brainstem nuclei that turn it into the clinical triad. Naloxone reverses every branch because it acts at the same receptor.
The μ-opioid receptor crystal structure, bound to a morphinan antagonist — this is essentially what naloxone binding looks like: it occupies the pocket without triggering the G-protein conformational change.
Protein Data Bank, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons (Mu-opioid receptor.jpg)
Papaver somniferum latex — the origin of morphine and codeine. Everything downstream (semi-synthetics like oxycodone and heroin, and fully synthetic fentanyl and its analogs) is an attempt to make this molecule hit μ harder and faster.
KGM007, Public domain — Wikimedia Commons (Opium pod cut to demonstrate fluid extraction1.jpg)
This single cascade tells you what every drug in this guide does. Naloxone is a competitive antagonist — it out-competes the agonist for the pocket and reverses all of it (including the analgesia and, in a dependent patient, the suppression of withdrawal). Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with the highest μ affinity of any of these drugs: it grips the receptor tightly but only partially activates it, so it relieves craving and withdrawal while its submaximal effect on the pre-Bötzinger complex gives it a respiratory ceiling. Methadone is a full agonist with a very long, variable half-life — full receptor activation with no ceiling, which is why it works for maintenance and why it kills during careless titration. Naltrexone is a long-acting antagonist that simply blocks the pocket for weeks.
⏱️

Know your agonist — potency, onset, and the duration that outlives naloxone

The single most consequential number in an overdose is not potency — it is duration. Naloxone's plasma half-life is roughly 30–90 minutes; its clinical effect lasts about 45–180 minutes depending on route and dose. (No FDA label states a duration — this is pharmacology, not a labelled figure.) Almost every opioid your patient took lasts longer than that. That mismatch is the entire reason people are found dead after a "successful" reversal.

Duration of action: naloxone versus the agonists it has to outlast. Everything below the green bars can re-sedate a patient after naloxone wears off.
AgentClassOnset / durationWhat makes it dangerous
Illicit fentanylSynthetic full agonistIV seconds–minutes; clinical effect 1–2 hExtremely lipophilic → crosses into brain almost instantly, so overdose happens before anyone can react. Redistributes out of fat afterward, producing rebound. Dominates the US illicit supply and drives the bulk of deaths. Can cause chest-wall (truncal) rigidity, which makes bag-mask ventilation fail.
Carfentanil & nitazenesUltra-potent syntheticsRapid; variable, often prolongedOrders of magnitude more potent than fentanyl. Frequently need much larger cumulative naloxone doses and an infusion.
Heroin (diacetylmorphine)Semi-synthetic prodrugIV 1–5 min; 3–5 hRapidly deacetylated to 6-MAM then morphine. Increasingly adulterated with fentanyl — the patient often does not know what they took.
MorphineNatural full agonistPO 30 min; 4–6 hActive metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide accumulates in renal failure → delayed, prolonged toxicity in CKD/ESRD. Histamine release → itching, flushing, hypotension.
Oxycodone / hydrocodone / hydromorphoneSemi-synthetic full agonistsIR 4–6 h; ER 12 hExtended-release products keep releasing drug for 12 h. A single naloxone "wake-up" dose is never sufficient — these patients need observation and often an infusion.
MethadoneFull agonist + NMDA antagonist + monoamine reuptake inhibitorOnset 30 min; analgesia 4–8 h but elimination t½ 8–59 hThe half-life vastly exceeds the analgesic duration, so the drug accumulates for days — deaths cluster around days 3–5 of initiation or dose increase. Also blocks hERG potassium channels → QTc prolongation and torsades.
BuprenorphinePartial agonist, very high μ affinitySL onset 30–60 min; 24–72 hIts affinity is so high it displaces full agonists — that is why it precipitates withdrawal, and why reversing a buprenorphine overdose can take unusually high naloxone doses. Conversely, its ceiling makes overdose in an opioid-tolerant adult uncommon.
TramadolWeak μ agonist + SNRIPO 1 h; 4–6 hThe opioid effect is minor; the danger is seizures and serotonin toxicity. Naloxone reverses the opioid component but does not treat the seizures and may even lower the seizure threshold further.
MeperidineFull agonist2–4 hMetabolite normeperidine is neuroexcitatory and renally cleared → tremor, myoclonus, seizures. Naloxone does not reverse normeperidine toxicity. Largely abandoned.
LoperamidePeripheral μ agonistVery long at supratherapeutic dosesNormally excluded from the CNS by P-glycoprotein, but massive doses ("poor man's methadone") saturate it. The lethal effect is cardiac: QRS widening and QTc prolongation → torsades and sudden death.
CodeineProdrug (CYP2D6 → morphine)4–6 hCYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers convert far more to morphine than expected — the basis of pediatric deaths after tonsillectomy and via breast milk. Poor metabolizers get no analgesia at all.
When you are handed "found down, gave Narcan, woke up," the very next question is what was the opioid and how long does it last? Heroin and IR oxycodone may genuinely be safe after a short observation. Methadone, extended-release products, buprenorphine, and body-packed drug are admissions — no exceptions.
⚗️

The modern supply — why the classic teaching now fails

The textbook opioid overdose — a heroin user who wakes up with 0.4 mg of naloxone and is fine — describes a drug supply that largely no longer exists. Three changes matter at the bedside:

Adulterant / trendWhat it isHow it changes your management
Illicitly manufactured fentanyl & analogsSynthetic μ agonists, now the dominant opioid in the US supply; also pressed into counterfeit "oxycodone"/"Xanax" pillsOnset is near-instant, so witnessed arrests are common. Higher cumulative naloxone doses are often needed. Fentanyl is not detected by standard urine opiate immunoassays — you must order a dedicated fentanyl assay.
Xylazine ("tranq")A veterinary α₂-adrenergic agonist — not an opioid at all. CDC SUDORS: among 21 jurisdictions the monthly proportion of illicitly-manufactured-fentanyl-involved deaths with xylazine detected rose 276%, from 2.9% (Jan 2019) to 10.9% (June 2022). DEA lab data: 30% of fentanyl powder seized in 2023 contained xylazine (up from 25% in 2022), versus 6% of fentanyl pillsNaloxone will not reverse it. Expect persistent sedation, bradycardia, and hypotension after the opioid component is reversed. The correct response is supportive: keep ventilating, do not chase it with escalating naloxone. Causes characteristic necrotic ulcers at and away from injection sites, and a withdrawal syndrome that responds to α₂ agonists rather than opioids.
Medetomidine — the 2025–26 successorAn α₂ agonist 100–200× more potent than xylazine. In Philadelphia it has now displaced xylazine: detected in 72% of illegal opioid samples tested in the last four months of 2024, while xylazine fell from 98% to 31% of samples over the same periodSame naloxone-resistant sedation — but the bigger problem is withdrawal. In the Philadelphia MMWR series (165 patients), median peak HR was 145 and SBP 195; the syndrome resisted opioids, benzodiazepines, clonidine, ketamine, olanzapine, and tizanidine. 91% needed ICU and 24% were intubated; 83% responded to a dexmedetomidine infusion (conventional doses of 0.2–1.5 mcg/kg/hr were used and titrated to effect — that upper figure is the top of the range reported, not a published ceiling). Notably it does not cause the classic tranq wounds — as it displaced xylazine, Philadelphia saw withdrawal visits rise while skin-infection visits fell.
Nitazenes (2-benzylbenzimidazoles)A chemically distinct class — not fentanyl analogs — several times more potent than fentanyl. By 2024 more new nitazenes than new fentanyl analogs were reported to UNODC, making up ~50% of reported opioid novel psychoactive substancesExpect multiple, large naloxone doses and plan for an infusion. They evade routine immunoassay entirely and can produce chest-wall rigidity like fentanyl.
Benzodiazepines & "designer" benzosCo-ingested, or pressed into counterfeit pillsAdditive respiratory depression. Naloxone reverses only the opioid share, so the patient may remain sedated. Do not reach for flumazenil.
Gabapentinoids, stimulantsGabapentin/pregabalin co-use; methamphetamine and cocaine co-involvement is risingGabapentinoids potentiate respiratory depression. Stimulant co-involvement produces a mixed picture — do not let a normal heart rate or normal-size pupils talk you out of an opioid overdose.
2 mg of fentanyl beside a penny. DEA's exact wording is that this "can be lethal depending on a person's body size, tolerance and past usage" — it is a potentially lethal quantity, not a human LD₅₀ (none exists). The scale is still the point: this is why counterfeit-pill overdoses are so often fatal on first exposure.
United States Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA)., Public domain — Wikimedia Commons (Fentanyl. 2 milligrams. A lethal dose in most people.jpg)
Lethal doses compared: heroin vs fentanyl vs carfentanil. Potency this extreme is why cumulative naloxone requirements have risen and why an infusion is so often needed.
United States Drug Enforcement Administration, Public domain — Wikimedia Commons (Heroin Carfentanil Fentanyl Lethal Dose Close Up.jpg)
Xylazine-associated necrotic ulcers. They characteristically appear at sites distant from injection, extend to deep tissue, and are frequently the reason the patient is admitted — screen every fentanyl-era injector for them.
Bhavani Nagendra Papudesi, MD, CC BY 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons (Xylazine-induced Abdominal Wounds.jpg)
The three waves of the US opioid epidemic — prescription opioids, then heroin, then synthetic opioids. CDC/NCHS provisional counts show ~70,400 overdose deaths in 2025, down ~13.5% from 81,313 in 2024 — a third consecutive annual decline and the lowest count since 2019. Synthetic opioids (ICD-10 T40.4, overwhelmingly illicit fentanyl) fell 48,913 → ~38,300, and heroin-involved deaths have collapsed to roughly 2,000 a year. Methadone was the only drug class to rise in 2025 (3,285 → 3,542). Provisional counts are revised monthly, so treat all of these as estimates. The epidemic is receding, but lethality per exposure has not fallen and the adulterant picture has grown more complex.
en:Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ., Public domain — Wikimedia Commons (3 waves of opioid overdose deaths. US timeline.png)
A patient who does not wake after 10 mg of cumulative naloxone almost certainly does not have a pure opioid overdose. Stop escalating and go looking: xylazine or another α₂ agonist, benzodiazepines or alcohol, hypoglycemia, hypoxic-ischemic brain injury from a prolonged down-time, head trauma, post-ictal state, CNS infection, or a second toxidrome entirely.

The toxidromes — pattern recognition

🗺️

The map — pupils, vitals, and the skin that breaks the tie

A toxidrome is a constellation of vital signs and physical findings that points to a receptor class rather than a specific molecule. You will almost never have a drug level in time to act on. What you will have, within thirty seconds of walking in, is a set of vitals, a pupil size, a skin exam, and bowel sounds — and that is enough to choose an antidote.

Work it in three steps: pupils put you on the left or right of the map, vital signs put you high or low, and then skin and bowel sounds break the tie inside a quadrant.

The toxidrome map. Note the two axes are almost independent: opioid and cholinergic both give you miosis and a depressed patient, and only the skin separates them at the door.
Miosis. The pupil in opioid toxicity is small and typically still reactive. It is the most recognizable leg of the triad — and the least reliable one.
Waster, CC BY 2.5 — Wikimedia Commons (Miosis.jpg)
Mydriasis (here from LSD). Big pupils push you to the right of the map — sympathomimetic, anticholinergic, or serotonin syndrome — and the skin exam then tells you which.
Thomas Bonini, CC0 — Wikimedia Commons (Mydriasis due to LSD usage.jpg)

The mnemonics worth actually keeping

  • Anticholinergic: "Mad as a hatter (delirium), blind as a bat (mydriasis and cycloplegia), red as a beet (flushing), hot as a hare (hyperthermia), dry as a bone (anhidrosis), the bowel and bladder lose their tone (ileus, retention), and the heart runs alone (tachycardia)."
  • Cholinergic — muscarinic: SLUDGE-M — Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis, Miosis. Expanded as DUMBBBELLSS — Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bronchospasm, Bradycardia, Bronchorrhea, Emesis, Lacrimation, Lethargy, Sweating, Salivation.
  • Cholinergic — the "Killer B's": Bronchorrhea, Bronchospasm, Bradycardia. These are what actually kill in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning, and they are the endpoint you titrate atropine against.
  • Cholinergic — nicotinic: MTWtHF ("days of the week") — Mydriasis, Tachycardia, Weakness, Hypertension, Fasciculations. Nicotinic effects oppose the muscarinic ones, which is exactly why an organophosphate patient can be tachycardic with big pupils and still be drowning in their own secretions.
Serotonin syndrome vs NMS — three questions. (1) Time course? Serotonin syndrome starts within 24 hours of adding or increasing a serotonergic drug; NMS evolves over days to weeks after a dopamine antagonist (or abrupt withdrawal of a dopamine agonist). (2) Tone or clonus? Serotonin syndrome gives hyperreflexia and clonus that is worse in the lower limbs; NMS gives global "lead-pipe" rigidity with hyporeflexia. (3) Bowel? Hyperactive with diarrhea in serotonin syndrome; normal or decreased in NMS.
The fastest bedside discriminator between the two hyperthermic delirium states — anticholinergic and cholinergic — is the axilla. Anticholinergic is bone dry; cholinergic is soaked. You can make that call before the monitor finishes cycling.
Toxidromes are patterns, not laws. Polysubstance exposure blurs every one of them, and mixed opioid-plus-stimulant use is now the norm rather than the exception. A normal heart rate or a mid-size pupil does not exclude opioid overdose. If the respiratory rate is low and the patient is obtunded, treat for opioid — naloxone is diagnostic as well as therapeutic, and it is far safer than waiting.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Signs & symptoms — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Read this table as three tiers. The triad — depressed consciousness, respiratory depression, miosis — is what makes the diagnosis. The complications are what turn a reversible poisoning into an ICU admission. And the absent findings matter too: a patient who is hypertensive, tachycardic, and diaphoretic is telling you something else is going on.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Depressed level of consciousness (somnolence → coma)~90%MOR agonism in cortex, thalamus, and the ascending reticular activating system suppresses arousal. Deepened further by the hypercapnia the same drug causes — CO₂ narcosis compounds the direct sedation.
Respiratory depression (bradypnea → apnea)~85%The lethal finding. Silencing of the MOR-rich pre-Bötzinger complex drops the respiratory rate, while blunting of the medullary CO₂ response removes the corrective reflex. Tidal volume falls too — so counting a "normal" rate can still mislead you.
Miosis (pinpoint pupils)~75%Disinhibition of the Edinger–Westphal nucleus → unopposed parasympathetic tone to the iris sphincter. Absent with meperidine, tramadol, and propoxyphene, lost with severe hypoxia or a co-ingested stimulant, and reversed to mydriasis once hypoxic brain injury sets in.
Decreased or absent bowel sounds / ileus~60%MOR agonism in the myenteric plexus slows propulsive motility. Clinically this also means co-ingestants absorb late — a reason a patient can deteriorate hours after presentation.
Hypoxia (SpO₂ <90%)~50%Hypoventilation → alveolar hypoxia. Worsened by any atelectasis, aspiration, or pulmonary edema layered on top.
Bradycardia~40%Increased vagal tone plus, in severe cases, direct hypoxic myocardial depression. A co-ingested α₂ agonist (xylazine, medetomidine) makes it much more pronounced and naloxone-resistant.
Hypotension~40%Histamine release (prominent with morphine and heroin) causing vasodilation, reduced sympathetic outflow, and — late — hypoxic cardiac depression.
Hypothermia~30%Environmental exposure during a prolonged down-time plus impaired central thermoregulation and shivering.
Aspiration / new infiltrate~20–30%Loss of protective airway reflexes with a full stomach; frequently worsened by naloxone-induced vomiting in a patient who is still not fully awake.
Track marks, abscesses, cellulitis~20–30%Repeated non-sterile injection. Look between toes, in the groin, and in the neck when the arms look clean.
Rhabdomyolysis (CK elevation)~15–20%Prolonged immobility on a limb → direct pressure necrosis, plus ischemia from compromised perfusion. Suspect it in anyone found down for hours.
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema~1%Increased pulmonary capillary permeability (hypoxia, histamine), negative-pressure edema from inspiring against a closed glottis, and a catecholamine surge causing pulmonary venoconstriction. Older series quote anywhere from 0.2% to 10% because case definitions differ wildly; two modern cohorts (n=1,831 and n=962) put it near 1.1%, and fentanyl does not appear to raise the rate. Presents with pink frothy sputum, usually within 4 hours.
Seizures<5%Rarely from the opioid itself — think tramadol, meperidine (normeperidine), profound hypoxia, or a co-ingestant. A seizing "opioid overdose" should make you widen the differential immediately.
Chest-wall (truncal) rigidity — "wooden chest"~13–15%*Rapid, high-dose fentanyl and analogs. The effect is centrally mediated (μ-receptor → locus coeruleus → noradrenergic α₁ outflow); fentanyl has no direct action on skeletal muscle. Direct laryngoscopic study shows the dominant barrier is closure of the vocal cords and upper airway, with true chest-wall and diaphragmatic rigidity adding to it — which is why bag-mask ventilation fails but an endotracheal tube restores compliance. Treat with a neuromuscular blocker, not escalating naloxone. *No true denominator exists for illicit overdose: a supervised-injection-site series recorded rigidity in 15.2% of 1,581 overdoses, and Massachusetts witnesses described body stiffening in 13%; in rapid high-dose anesthetic induction the incidence is 50–90%+. Treat the percentage as an order of magnitude, not a rate.
Compartment syndrome<5%Prolonged compression of a limb → tissue pressure exceeds perfusion pressure. Gluteal, thigh, and forearm compartments are the classic sites.
Frequencies vary widely across published cohorts because case definitions differ (prehospital vs ED, fatal vs non-fatal, heroin-era vs fentanyl-era). Treat these as relative weightings for pattern recognition, not as epidemiologic constants.
🧪

Reading the labs — what each value is telling you

There is no lab that diagnoses opioid overdose. The diagnosis is clinical and the response to naloxone confirms it. Labs exist to find the complications and the mimics.

TestWhat it means, why it moves, and what fools it
Fingerstick glucoseThe first test, every time, before anything else. Severe hypoglycemia produces confusion, slurred speech, seizures, and coma — an exact phenocopy of opioid overdose, and it is instantly reversible. Opioids themselves are associated with hypoglycemia (adjusted reporting odds ratio ~1.53; tramadol is the classic offender). Check it, and check it again if the picture changes.
Venous or arterial blood gasThe test that actually quantifies the poisoning. Expect an acute respiratory acidosis: high pCO₂ with low pH and a normal-ish bicarbonate. A pCO₂ >60 with pH <7.20 in a patient not improving on naloxone is an intubation. A superimposed metabolic acidosis (elevated lactate, anion gap) signals tissue hypoperfusion, seizure, or a co-ingestant — widen the differential.
Capnography (EtCO₂)Not strictly a lab, but the single most useful continuous number you have. It measures ventilation, whereas pulse oximetry measures oxygenation. See the pearl below — on supplemental oxygen these diverge dangerously.
Urine drug screenFar less useful than people assume, and actively misleading if misread. The standard opiate immunoassay detects morphine-class compounds; fentanyl is a phenylpiperidine and does not cross-react. Methadone, buprenorphine, oxycodone, tramadol, and the nitazenes each need a dedicated assay. A negative opiate screen in an overdose tells you essentially nothing. Order a fentanyl-specific assay explicitly. It also cannot distinguish recent from remote use, so it never overrides the clinical picture.
Creatine kinase (CK)Rises with rhabdomyolysis from prolonged down-time. Diagnostic threshold is >5× the upper limit of normal (or >1,000 IU/L); many protocols use >5,000 U/L to trigger aggressive fluids. Peaks at 24–72 h, so a normal initial value in a patient found down does not exclude it — repeat it.
Creatinine, potassium, phosphate, calciumAKI from myoglobin, hypovolemia, or hypoperfusion. Rhabdomyolysis releases intracellular contents → hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia with hypocalcemia (calcium precipitates with phosphate). Hyperkalemia here is the acute threat to life.
Acetaminophen and salicylate levelsMandatory in any intentional overdose, and reasonable in any undifferentiated one, because both are silent early and lethal late — and both are treatable if caught. Many opioid products are combination pills containing acetaminophen.
ECGLook for two things. A long QTc points to methadone (or a QT-prolonging co-ingestant); ≥500 ms is the action threshold. A wide QRS (>100 ms) means sodium-channel blockade — think TCA or massive loperamide, and it changes your management entirely (bicarbonate, and physostigmine becomes contraindicated).
LactateElevated from hypoxia, hypoperfusion, or seizure. A rising lactate in a "stable" post-overdose patient should prompt a hunt for occult ischemia, sepsis, or compartment syndrome.
TroponinMild elevation is common from hypoxic demand ischemia. A large or rising value suggests a genuine coronary event — relevant in stimulant co-use, where vasospasm is a real mechanism.
CBC, blood cultures, HIV/HCV/HBV serologiesIn anyone who injects: leukocytosis and fever mean blood cultures ×2 and an echocardiogram until endocarditis is excluded. Screening serologies are a standard-of-care opportunity you will not get again if the patient leaves.
Pregnancy testIn anyone who can become pregnant — it changes the entire treatment plan (see the comorbidities module).
EtCO₂ beats SpO₂, and never more so than on supplemental oxygen. Pulse oximetry reports oxygenation, and it lags — by up to 2–3 minutes when oxygen is running. A patient on 2 L nasal cannula can sit at SpO₂ 98% while their pCO₂ climbs toward 80. In procedural-sedation studies respiratory depression was roughly 17.6× more likely to be detected by capnography than by oximetry. Putting a post-overdose patient on oxygen without capnography blinds the very monitor you were relying on.
🩻

Imaging — what to order, when, and what you are looking for

StudyWhen to order itFinding & what it means
Chest radiographAny hypoxemia, any suspicion of aspiration, any prolonged down-time, before ICU transferBilateral fluffy alveolar infiltrates with a normal heart size = noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Dependent-segment consolidation (posterior upper lobes / superior lower lobes if supine, basal if upright) = aspiration. A clear film early does not exclude either — both lag the physiology.
Bedside echocardiogram / POCUSWhen pulmonary edema is present and the cause is unclear, or in any febrile injectorDistinguishes noncardiogenic edema (normal EF, no B-line–predominant cardiogenic pattern, no elevated filling pressures) from cardiogenic edema. In a febrile person who injects drugs, look for vegetations — right-sided tricuspid disease is classic but left-sided disease is increasingly common.
CT head, non-contrastFailure to improve with naloxone, focal deficit, seizure, head trauma, or a prolonged unexplained comaExcludes hemorrhage, ischemic stroke, and traumatic injury — all of which mimic or accompany overdose. Diffuse loss of grey–white differentiation and sulcal effacement after a prolonged arrest indicates hypoxic-ischemic injury (a finding to interpret with great caution, not to prognosticate from early).
CT abdomen/pelvisAny suspicion of body packing or stuffingShows the packets. Plain abdominal films miss packets — a negative KUB in a suspected packer is not clearance. Confirm with CT plus documented packet-free stools.
Extremity imaging / compartment pressuresTense, painful limb after a prolonged down-timeCompartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis supported by measurement: delta pressure = diastolic BP − compartment pressure; <30 mmHg is a fasciotomy. Do not wait for pulselessness, and do not wait for the CK.
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema pattern — diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacification with a normal cardiac silhouette (neurogenic case illustrated; opioid-associated NCPE produces the same appearance). The management contrast with cardiogenic edema is the highest-yield teaching point on this page: PEEP and oxygen, not diuresis.
Moustafa A. Mansour, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons (Neurogenic Pulmonary Edema.jpg)
Foreign-body granulomatosis in a person who injects drugs — a pulmonary arteriole occluded by microcrystalline cellulose and talc from crushed oral tablets. Over time this produces pulmonary hypertension and a fixed diffusion defect, and it explains chronic dyspnea that will not resolve with the overdose.
Yale Rosen, CC BY-SA 2.0 — Wikimedia Commons (Foreign body embolism - IVDA.jpg)
🩺 Clinic — screening, MOUD, and preventing the next overdose
Assess

Recognizing risk & diagnosing OUD

🔍

Who is at risk, and how OUD actually presents in clinic

You will almost never see an overdose in clinic. What you will see is the person who is going to have one — and the visit where you can change that. The highest-yield populations are people prescribed opioids at higher doses, people with a prior overdose, people who inject, people recently released from incarceration or discharged from a controlled setting, and anyone whose tolerance has just dropped.

Loss of tolerance is the most under-appreciated risk factor in medicine. Release from jail, discharge from residential treatment or a hospital, or completion of a "detox" — all reset tolerance downward while the person's expected dose stays the same in their head. Withdrawal management without ongoing MOUD is associated with increased overdose death for exactly this reason. Both ASAM and CDC advise against detoxification without continued medication treatment.

Diagnosing opioid use disorder — DSM-5-TR

OUD requires ≥2 of 11 criteria within a 12-month period, causing clinically significant impairment or distress. Severity is simply the count: mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe ≥6. The criteria group into four clusters:

ClusterCriteria
Impaired controlTaken in larger amounts or over a longer period than intended; persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down; a great deal of time spent obtaining, using, or recovering; craving.
Social impairmentFailure to fulfil major role obligations; continued use despite social or interpersonal problems; important activities given up or reduced.
Risky useRecurrent use in physically hazardous situations; continued use despite knowing it is causing a physical or psychological problem.
PharmacologicTolerance; withdrawal.
The two pharmacologic criteria — tolerance and withdrawal — do not count when a patient is taking opioids solely as prescribed under appropriate medical supervision. A cancer patient physiologically dependent on morphine does not thereby have OUD. Conflating dependence with addiction is how patients get abandoned by their prescriber and end up buying fentanyl.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Outpatient workup before and during MOUD

PDMP queryAt initiation and periodically thereafter (many states mandate it). You are looking for multiple prescribers, overlapping benzodiazepines, and total daily MME — not for a reason to discharge the patient from your practice.Every visit
Urine drug testingBaseline and periodically. Order a fentanyl-specific assay — the standard opiate immunoassay will not detect it. CDC Recommendation 10 frames UDT as a tool to support care, not to punish; an unexpected result is a conversation, not a discharge.Baseline
HIV, HCV, HBV, syphilisIn anyone who injects, at baseline and periodically. Offer HBV vaccination, HCV treatment, and HIV PrEP at the same visit — this may be your only contact.Baseline
Pregnancy testIn anyone who can become pregnant, before starting MOUD — it changes agent selection and rules out naltrexone.Baseline
LFTsBaseline and periodically for naltrexone (the boxed hepatotoxicity warning has been removed, but monitoring remains prudent) and for buprenorphine in patients with hepatitis C.Baseline
ECG for QTcMethadone only — before treatment, at ~1 month, annually, before any titration above 100 mg/day, and 7 days after such a titration.If methadone
CBC, BMPBaseline general assessment; renal function guides gabapentinoid dosing and opioid selection.Baseline
Wound assessmentEvery visit in anyone who injects. Xylazine-associated ulcers occur at sites away from injection and are frequently hidden under clothing — you have to look.Every visit
Treat

Medications for OUD — the ladder

💊

Choosing the agent, then dosing it properly

The ASAM National Practice Guideline (2020 Focused Update — still the current version) is explicit that all three FDA-approved medications should be available to all patients, and that choice depends on patient preference, treatment history, current illness severity, and setting. There is no universal first-line; there is a best fit.

What is not negotiable: medication beats no medication. Larochelle's 2018 cohort of 17,568 Massachusetts adults who survived an overdose found methadone and buprenorphine each associated with substantial reductions in all-cause and opioid-related mortality — and that only a minority of survivors received either.

The ceiling effect, drawn. A full agonist's effect keeps climbing with dose until breathing stops. Buprenorphine plateaus — which is why it is the safest of the three in an unsupervised setting, and why it is the drug you can send home with a month of refills.
Vanwa71, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons (Buprenorphine is a Partial Agonist at the μ-Opioid Receptor.png)
Buprenorphine/naloxone sublingual film. The naloxone component is poorly absorbed sublingually and is there only to deter injection — it contributes nothing therapeutically when the film is taken as directed.
Sintegral, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons (8-2 Suboxone 1.jpg)
1
Buprenorphine–naloxone — the default for most outpatients
Office-based, no X-waiver needed since the MAT Act, and a respiratory ceiling that makes it survivable
▾
Buprenorphine is a partial μ agonist with the highest receptor affinity of any drug in this guide. High affinity means it occupies and holds the receptor (suppressing craving and withdrawal, and blocking the effect of any full agonist taken on top). Partial activation means the respiratory depression plateaus — the dose–response curve flattens instead of climbing to apnea. That combination is why it can be dispensed for home use at all.
Know the limits of the ceiling — it is real, but narrower than the teaching suggests. The human evidence is ~40 healthy, opioid-naïve volunteers given low intravenous doses (max 0.6 mg/70 kg), measuring hypercapnic ventilation under a CO₂ clamp (Dahan, Br J Anaesth 2005/2006): ventilation plateaued at about 50% of baseline, while fentanyl progressed to apnea. Four caveats matter at the bedside: (1) it has never been demonstrated at the systemic exposures of 8–24 mg daily maintenance; (2) the FDA label states that benzodiazepines alter the usual ceiling, making buprenorphine's respiratory effects "appear similar to those of full opioid agonists" — most buprenorphine deaths involve injected tablets plus a sedative; (3) it may not apply to children, where a fatal unintentional ingestion is documented; and (4) when buprenorphine does depress respiration it is naloxone-resistant — roughly 1.2 mg/70 kg for 50% reversal and 2.5 mg/70 kg for 80%, which is why an infusion rather than boluses is required. The ceiling justifies unsupervised dispensing; it does not mean overdose is impossible.

Standard ("traditional") initiation — requires objective withdrawal first

The patient must be in genuine withdrawal before the first dose, or buprenorphine's high affinity will strip the full agonist off the receptor and precipitate withdrawal. Conventionally that means COWS ≥8–12, roughly 12–24 h after a short-acting opioid and 48–72 h after methadone. In the fentanyl era many programs wait for COWS ≥12–13, because fentanyl stored in fat keeps re-entering the circulation.

StepDoseWhat you are doing
Day 1 — first dose2 mg/0.5 mg or 4 mg/1 mg SLTest dose once COWS threshold is met. Observe 60–90 min.
Day 1 — titration+2 to +4 mg at ~2-hour intervalsTitrate to symptom relief, not to a target number.
Day 1 — typical totalup to 8 mg/2 mgLabel-conservative day-1 ceiling; many programs go higher (see rung 2).
Day 216 mg/4 mg SL once dailyConsolidate to a single daily dose.
Maintenance target16 mg/dayThe dose at which most patients have full craving suppression and near-complete receptor occupancy.
Label maximum24 mg/dayHistorically framed as a hard ceiling; 24–32 mg/day is used off-label at many fentanyl-era programs.
The 2024 label change matters. In December 2024 the FDA permitted removal of the statements that doses above 24 mg/day confer no clinical advantage and that 16 mg is a "target" — clarifying explicitly that the target dose is not a maximum daily maintenance dosage and that further upward titration may be necessary. If your fentanyl-exposed patient is still craving on 16 mg, the answer is usually more buprenorphine, not a different drug.

Low-dose ("microdose" / Bernese) initiation — the fentanyl-era workaround

The principle is elegant: start at a dose too small to displace the full agonist, escalate slowly while the full agonist continues, and stop the full agonist only once buprenorphine occupancy is high. No washout and no requirement to be in withdrawal. This is the strategy for the patient who cannot tolerate — or has already failed — a traditional induction.

DayBuprenorphine SLFull agonist
10.5 mg once (a quarter of a 2 mg tablet)Continue
20.5 mg twice dailyContinue
31 mg twice dailyContinue
42 mg twice dailyContinue
53 mg twice dailyContinue
64 mg twice dailyStop
712–16 mg daily—
Be honest about the evidenceMany schedule variants exist and starting doses as low as 0.2 mg have been used. The optimum schedule has not been defined, and a study of low-dose initiation in people using fentanyl found it effective for roughly one-third of participants. Offer it as a real option, not a solved problem.

Extended-release buprenorphine (Sublocade)

  • Standard regimen: two initial doses of 300 mg SC monthly, then 100 mg monthly maintenance; increase back to 300 mg monthly if benefits outweigh risks.
  • February 2025 label change — rapid initiation: may now be started after a single 4 mg dose of transmucosal buprenorphine plus a 1-hour observation period, rather than ≥7 days of daily sublingual dosing. In the supporting trial, second-injection receipt was 66.4% with rapid initiation versus 54.5% with the standard approach.
  • Also approved February 2025: alternative injection sites — abdomen, thigh, buttock, or the back of the upper arm.
  • Already stable on sublingual? Patients taking 8–24 mg daily transmucosal buprenorphine can transition directly to the 300 mg starting dose. Maintenance injections go at least 26 days apart.
  • Boxed warning — never give it intravenously. Sublocade forms a solid mass on contact with body fluids; IV administration can cause occlusion, local tissue damage, and life-threatening pulmonary embolism. It is dispensed only through a restricted REMS program.
  • The other extended-release option — Brixadi (approved May 2023): comes in weekly and monthly subcutaneous formulations, injected in the buttock, thigh, abdomen, or upper arm. The weekly product is useful for someone you want to see often, or who is not yet stable enough for a monthly commitment. Weekly doses cannot simply be added up to make a monthly dose — the formulations are not interchangeable that way.

Side effects and what to monitor

Constipation, nausea, headache, sweating, insomnia, and dental caries (a 2022 FDA warning specific to the sublingual route — counsel patients to rinse with water and not brush immediately after dosing). Precipitated withdrawal is the initiation-phase risk. Monitor LFTs in hepatitis C.

If intolerant or allergic: true buprenorphine allergy is rare. Intolerance of the naloxone component (or pregnancy) → use the buprenorphine monoproduct. Persistent nausea → try a different formulation (film vs tablet) or split dosing. Genuine failure → move to methadone, which has no ceiling and often succeeds where buprenorphine could not hold a very high-tolerance patient.
2
Methadone — for high tolerance, buprenorphine failure, or patient preference
Full agonist, no ceiling, opioid treatment program only — and the drug that kills on day 3, not day 1
▾
Methadone is a full μ agonist, so there is no ceiling on either its benefit or its respiratory depression. It additionally antagonises NMDA receptors and inhibits monoamine reuptake. For OUD it must be dispensed through a federally certified opioid treatment program (OTP) — unlike buprenorphine, it cannot be prescribed from a general office.

Dosing under the 2024 federal rule

The 42 CFR Part 8 final rule (published 2 Feb 2024, effective 2 Apr 2024) substantially rewrote methadone practice in recognition of fentanyl-driven tolerance:

ParameterValueNotes
Day-1 total doseShould not exceed 50 mgRaised from the prior limits, and the 30 mg initial-dose cap was deleted from the CFR entirely. Exceeding 50 mg requires a documented medical rationale (e.g. a verified transfer at a higher dose). Know the conflict: the FDA label still reads "initial dose should not exceed 30 mg" and "first day should not ordinarily exceed 40 mg." Dosing to the regulation's 50 mg is permitted but is a deviation from labelling that 42 CFR 8.12(h)(4) requires you to document.
Typical starting dose20–30 mgWith 5–10 mg additional for persistent withdrawal on day 1, monitoring for sedation.
Titration increment5–15 mg every 3–5 daysHigh-risk patients: no more than 20 mg increase per week. This is the safety-critical number.
Effective maintenance80–120 mg/day per the FDA labelThe label states "most commonly, clinical stability is achieved at doses between 80 to 120 mg/day." 60–120 mg/day is widely taught but is not the labelled range. Many fentanyl-era patients need the upper end or beyond. Steady state takes 3–5 days at any given dose.
Take-home dosesDays 1–14: up to 7 days · Days 15–30: up to 14 days · Day 31+: up to 28 daysThe new phased schedule, a major liberalization from the pre-2024 rules.
Methadone kills on days 3–10, not day 1. Analgesic duration is 6–8 hours but the elimination half-life reaches 59 hours, so the patient feels under-dosed while drug silently accumulates. Deaths characteristically occur at home, during sleep, many hours after the peak serum level. The risk of fatal drug toxicity in the first two weeks of induction has been estimated at 6.7× that of untreated heroin users and 98× that of long-term maintenance patients. Titrate slowly, and warn every single patient about the first fortnight.

Monitoring

QTc — methadone blocks hERG potassium channels. A systematic review found QTc prolongation in about 34% of maintenance patients with a pooled torsades incidence of 2%. ECG before treatment, at ~1 month, annually, before titrating above 100 mg/day, and 7 days after. QTc 450–500 ms → monitor more closely and inform the patient; QTc >500 ms → reduce or discontinue. Note the provenance: the FDA label carries a boxed warning for "Life-Threatening QT Prolongation" but states no millisecond threshold at all — the 450/500 ms numbers come from expert consensus (Krantz et al., Ann Intern Med 2009), not from the label. Keep K⁺ ≥4.0 and Mg²⁺ ≥2.0.

If QTc becomes the limiting factor: switch to buprenorphine (minimal QT effect) rather than abandoning treatment. Also review and remove stacked QT-prolonging drugs before giving up on methadone.
3
Naltrexone — for the patient who is already opioid-free and declines agonists
Pure antagonist. Excellent once started; the problem is getting started
▾
Naltrexone is a long-acting competitive antagonist — it simply occupies μ and blocks anything the patient takes on top. No agonist effect means no euphoria, no dependence, and no diversion value, but also no withdrawal relief and no craving suppression from receptor activation.
FormulationStartTarget / maintenanceRequirement
Oral naltrexone25 mg (half tablet)50 mg PO daily if no withdrawal signsAdherence-dependent — the main reason it underperforms.
XR naltrexone (Vivitrol)380 mg IM gluteal every 4 weeks, alternating buttocksRemoves the daily adherence problem entirely.
The washout is the whole problem — and the required interval depends on which opioid, with the major sources disagreeing. The FDA label specifies a minimum of 7–10 opioid-free days for short-acting opioids and warns that patients coming off buprenorphine or methadone stay vulnerable for as long as two weeks. SAMHSA TIP 63 says 7–10 days short-acting, 10–14 days long-acting. ASAM 2020 is shorter still — about 6 days short-acting and 7–10 days long-acting — which is below the labelled minimum, and ASAM contradicts itself elsewhere with 7–14 days after buprenorphine. When in doubt, wait longer and use the label. Get this wrong and you precipitate severe withdrawal. A naloxone challenge can confirm they are no longer physically dependent. This is exactly what the X:BOT trial quantified: once initiated, XR-naltrexone performed comparably to buprenorphine–naloxone — but 28% could not be inducted onto it at all, versus 6% for buprenorphine. In intention-to-treat terms, buprenorphine wins because more patients actually start.
Do not initiate naltrexone in pregnancy. If a patient is already stable on it before conceiving, continuation is a shared decision. Also counsel every patient that tolerance falls while blocked — a relapse after stopping naltrexone carries a high overdose risk.
4
Wrap-around care — what makes the medication work
Everything that stops the patient dying of something other than the next dose
▾
  • Take-home naloxone for every patient and, ideally, a household member — see the module below.
  • Syringe services program referral; fentanyl and xylazine test strips where legally available.
  • Never use alone counseling — including the national overdose-prevention hotlines.
  • Treat the psychiatric comorbidity. Untreated depression, PTSD, and ADHD drive relapse, and MOUD should never be withheld pending psychiatric stabilization.
  • Hepatitis C treatment — cure rates are excellent and active use is not a contraindication.
  • Contingency management and peer recovery support where available.
Prevent

Take-home naloxone — prescribe it like a seatbelt

💉

Which product, and how to teach it

Walley's 2013 BMJ study is the evidence that makes this routine care: across 19 Massachusetts communities, overdose education and naloxone distribution was associated with a 46% reduction in the overdose death rate in communities with enrollment above 100 per 100,000. This is a population-level mortality intervention that costs a prescription.

ProductDose & routeStatusWhen to pick it
Narcan nasal spray4 mg intranasal, 1 spray per nostrilOTC (first OTC naloxone, approved March 2023)The default. No prescription barrier, no needle, minimal training.
Generic naloxone NS4 mg INOTCSame as above, lower cost.
RiVive3 mg INOTCLower-dose intranasal option.
Kloxxado8 mg INPrescriptionHigher nominal dose — but not shown to save more lives. See the pearl below before reaching for it.
Rezenopy10 mg INPrescriptionHighest available intranasal dose.
Zimhi5 mg IM/SC prefilled syringePrescriptionHigh-dose injectable for a trained caregiver.
Generic naloxone vial0.4 mg/mL or 1 mg/mLPrescriptionCheapest, but requires drawing up — the highest-friction option for a layperson in a panic.
Correct intranasal technique. Support the neck, tilt the head back, insert the nozzle until fingers touch the nose, and press the plunger firmly. One spray delivers the full dose — there is nothing to prime and nothing to test-spray.
Eldridge Misnomer, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons (Narcan Administration.svg)
Prefilled parenteral naloxone. In clinical settings the IV route allows the fine titration that matters in a dependent patient — small increments to breathing, rather than a single large dose to wakefulness.
Intropin, CC BY 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons (Naloxone (1).JPG)
The counseling script — say all five
  1. Give two doses — carry two, because one is often not enough with fentanyl.
  2. Call 911 first or immediately after the first dose.
  3. Give rescue breaths — this is the part everyone skips, and it is the part that works.
  4. If there is no response in 2–3 minutes, give the second dose.
  5. Warn them the person may wake up agitated, may vomit, and may become sleepy again — stay with them and do not let them use again.
Bigger is not better — resist the milligram arms race. Every current naloxone nasal-spray label now carries this sentence: "All approved naloxone hydrochloride products achieve plasma concentrations that have been shown to be efficacious in reversing the effects of opioid overdose. Comparing different products on a nominal mg-for-mg basis may be misleading." The only comparative field data agree — in a New York law-enforcement series (MMWR 2024), 8 mg intranasal gave no survival advantage over 4 mg and did not reduce the number of doses needed, but carried 2.51× the risk of withdrawal signs including vomiting (95% CI 1.51–4.18). Vomiting in someone not yet protecting their airway is its own hazard. 4 mg intranasal remains the sensible default; choose a higher-dose product for a specific reason, not reflexively because fentanyl is involved.
Prescribe naloxone to the household, not just the patient — the person overdosing cannot self-administer. And offer it at ≥50 MME/day regardless of whether OUD is present. A chronic-pain patient with sleep apnea on 60 MME is a legitimate naloxone candidate.
Prescribe

Prescribing opioids safely — CDC 2022

📋

The guideline, and the way it is most often misapplied

The CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain (2022) replaced the 2016 version specifically because the 2016 thresholds were being applied as rigid rules — triggering forced tapers, abrupt discontinuations, and patient abandonment. The 2022 document deliberately softened the numeric framing.

  • Prescribe the lowest effective dose for the expected duration of pain warranting an opioid; maximize non-opioid and non-pharmacologic therapy first.
  • Use caution at any dose, and take particular care when increasing to ≥50 MME/day; carefully justify doses at higher levels rather than treating a number as a hard cap.
  • Evaluate benefits and risks within 1–4 weeks of starting, then periodically.
  • Offer naloxone when risk factors are present — higher dosage, history of overdose or substance use disorder, or concurrent benzodiazepine use.
  • Avoid concurrent benzodiazepine prescribing where possible (FDA boxed warning, 2016).
  • Do not abruptly discontinue opioids in a physically dependent patient — forced tapers are associated with overdose and suicide.
  • Check the PDMP and use urine drug testing to support care.

Morphine milligram equivalents — use the calculator, know the traps

MME lets you compare total daily opioid burden across agents. The commonly used oral conversion factors are morphine 1, hydrocodone 1, oxycodone 1.5, oxymorphone 3, codeine 0.15. The 2022 update revised the factors for hydromorphone, tramadol, and methadone specifically — so a calculator built on 2016 factors will give you a different (and now outdated) answer for those three.

Never convert methadone or transmucosal fentanyl with a simple multiplier. Methadone's conversion factor is non-linear (it rises with the daily dose) and its long half-life makes any equivalence estimate unreliable; transmucosal fentanyl products each have their own factor and are not interchangeable. Use a validated calculator — MDCalc's MME calculator is maintained against the CDC 2022 guideline — and consult pain or palliative care for methadone rotations. Buprenorphine is deliberately excluded from MME calculators because its ceiling means it does not carry dose-dependent overdose risk in the same way.
Score

🧮

The initiation threshold is moving. Conventional teaching is COWS ≥8 before the first buprenorphine dose, and many fentanyl-era protocols wait for ≥12–13. But ED-INNOVATION (JAMA 2026, N=1,994) enrolled patients at COWS ≥4 and saw precipitated withdrawal in under 1% (0.6% vs 0.8%) despite 76% fentanyl positivity. Read that carefully: 4 was the eligibility threshold — the conventional 8-point threshold still governed in-ED dosing. The honest takeaway is not "start at 4," it is that initiating in the COWS 4–7 range proved far safer than the fentanyl-era fear suggested. Know your institution's protocol and which formulation you are starting.
SourceItems and point values per Wesson & Ling (J Psychoactive Drugs 2003), as published by NIDA and reproduced on MDCalc. Severity bands: 5–12 mild, 13–24 moderate, 25–36 moderately severe, >36 severe.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & whole-patient prevention

🛡️

Beyond USPSTF: offer hepatitis B vaccination, tetanus, pneumococcal and influenza vaccination, and — for anyone who injects — hepatitis C treatment (active use is not a contraindication), wound care, and syringe services referral.

Escalate

When clinic isn't enough

🚑

Red flags → same-day ED or admission

Send to the ED today for any of:
  • Fever in a person who injects drugs — this is endocarditis, epidural abscess, or septic arthritis until proven otherwise. It needs blood cultures ×2 and an echocardiogram, not an outpatient antibiotic.
  • Any witnessed or reported overdose since the last visit.
  • New or worsening skin/soft-tissue wounds — xylazine-associated ulcer, abscess, or any suspicion of necrotizing infection.
  • Severe untreated withdrawal the patient cannot manage as an outpatient, or autonomic instability suggesting α₂-agonist (medetomidine) withdrawal.
  • Suicidality, or an overdose with stated intent.
  • Methadone dose escalation with syncope, palpitations, or QTc ≥500 ms.
  • Pregnancy with untreated OUD — urgent, because abrupt withdrawal risks preterm labor and fetal demise.
Escalating dose requests, lost prescriptions, and multiple prescribers on the PDMP are signals to intensify treatment — reassess for OUD, offer MOUD, tighten follow-up — not signals to discharge the patient from your practice. Abandonment reliably pushes people to the illicit supply, which now means fentanyl.
🛏️ Wards — reversal, observation, withdrawal, and the discharge that prevents the next one
Resuscitate

The acute reversal — airway first

⛑️

What to do in the first five minutes

Ventilation comes before naloxone. The AHA 2023 Focused Update is unambiguous: "the cornerstone of treatment is highly effective CPR and ventilation… For patients who definitely have a pulse (i.e. respiratory arrest), rescue breathing or bag-mask ventilation should be performed until effective spontaneous breathing occurs." Naloxone takes 1–3 minutes to work. Bag-mask ventilation works immediately, and it is what prevents the hypoxic brain injury that naloxone cannot undo.
The opioid-associated emergency pathway. Note where naloxone sits — after the airway, not before it — and note that the algorithm does not end at "patient woke up."

Naloxone dosing

SettingStartTitrationCeiling / next step
AHA 2023 antidote table0.2–2 mg IV/IO/IM
or 2–4 mg intranasal		Repeat every 2–3 min as needed, titrating to "reversal of respiratory depression and restoration of protective airway reflexes"Infusion at ⅔ of the waking dose per hour
Known/suspected opioid dependence0.04–0.05 mg IVRepeat every 1–2 min, doubling as needed, until the patient is ventilating adequatelyThe low-dose approach exists to avoid precipitated withdrawal. More than half of medical toxicology sources recommend a starting dose <0.05 mg IV in this population.
Apneic / periarrest0.4–2 mg IV (or 4 mg IN if no access)Double every 2–3 minDo not under-dose a dying patient to protect them from withdrawal.
Pediatric0.1 mg/kgRepeat q2–3 minSame infusion principle
Suspected fentanyl analog / nitazene0.4–2 mg IVEscalate rapidlyPrepare for a cumulative total of at least 10 mg. Have an infusion ready before you need it.
Titrate to breathing, not to consciousness. The endpoint is a respiratory rate ≥12 with adequate tidal volume and a normal EtCO₂ — not an awake, angry, vomiting patient. Over-reversal buys you agitation, aspiration, a catecholamine surge, and a real risk of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and it destroys any chance of starting the patient on MOUD in the same encounter. The AHA makes the corollary explicit: patients with opioid overdose "who are breathing normally with intact airway reflexes can be carefully observed without naloxone, regardless of somnolence."
If you cannot bag-mask ventilate a patient with a patent airway, think fentanyl chest-wall rigidity ("wooden chest"). This is a centrally mediated rise in truncal muscle tone after rapid high-dose fentanyl or an analog. Naloxone reverses the central respiratory suppression but may not reverse the rigidity. The answer is a neuromuscular blocker and definitive airway control — do not keep pushing naloxone while the patient desaturates.
Naloxone in cardiac arrest. The AHA states naloxone has no known or theoretical benefit once the patient is in cardiac arrest — respiratory support and high-quality CPR are the treatment. But it also says that if there is uncertainty whether the patient is in cardiac or only respiratory arrest, naloxone should be given. In practice: if you are unsure, give it, and never let it delay compressions.
Admit

Who to admit, and who can go home

📋

The observation decision

The central question after a reversal is not "are they awake?" It is "will the opioid outlast the naloxone?" Look back at the duration chart in the pathophysiology section — that mismatch is what you are managing.

Admit for any of these

  • Persistent or recurrent respiratory depression after the initial reversal window
  • Required more than two naloxone doses, or any naloxone infusion
  • A long-acting opioid implicated — methadone, extended-release oxycodone or morphine, transdermal fentanyl patch, extended-release buprenorphine
  • Body packer or stuffer
  • Co-ingestion with a delayed-toxicity agent — acetaminophen, salicylate, TCA, sustained-release verapamil or diltiazem, bupropion ER
  • Aspiration, new hypoxemia, or a new infiltrate
  • Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, compartment syndrome, or a prolonged down-time
  • Suicidal intent
  • Inability to ambulate or protect the airway; social circumstances precluding safe discharge
Withdrawal that is severe enough to drive a patient out the door is itself an admission-level problem. A patient-directed discharge at hour 3 is how endocarditis goes untreated — treat the withdrawal aggressively and early, and the medical problem becomes manageable.
🧮

St. Paul's / HOUR one-hour observation rule

Derived at St. Paul's Hospital, Vancouver, and prospectively validated as the HOUR study (Clemency, Acad Emerg Med 2019, 538 patients). After naloxone reversal, a patient may be considered for discharge at one hour if all six criteria are normal. Check each box that is true:

Can ambulate as usual✓
SpO₂ >92% on room air✓
Respiratory rate >10 and <20/min✓
Temperature >35.0 °C and <37.5 °C✓
Heart rate >50 and <100 bpm✓
GCS 15✓
0
The rule is supportive, not dispositive. In the HOUR validation (n=538, 82 adverse events = 15.4%, no deaths within 48 h) the rule alone had sensitivity 84.1%, specificity 62.1%, and negative predictive value 95.6% — not 100%. Rule plus clinician gestalt together still missed adverse events in about 1.9% (10 of 529). It is a single-centre validation, is not endorsed by ACEP or AHA as a discharge standard, and was validated in a largely heroin-era cohort — fentanyl, nitazenes, and α₂-agonist adulterants all change the pretest probability. A patient can pass all six criteria and still need admission if they took methadone, an extended-release product, or an unknown substance.
Who needs longer observation regardless of the scoreMethadone (24–36 h monitored) · extended-release or long-acting formulations, including ingested or dermally applied fentanyl patches · buprenorphine overdose in an opioid-naïve patient or child · body packers and stuffers until confirmed clear · anyone who required repeat doses or an infusion · suspected nitazene or ultra-potent synthetic · renal or hepatic failure (metabolite accumulation) · all pediatric exposures. StatPearls advises 6–12 h of monitoring after reversal for longer-half-life opioids.
Orders

Admission order set

🧾

Treat

Withdrawal & starting MOUD inpatient

💊

The inpatient ladder

1
Start buprenorphine — this is the treatment, not the comfort measure
Monitored dosing is the advantage of being inpatient; use it
▾

Standard inpatient initiation: at COWS ≥8–12, give 4 mg SL, reassess at 60–90 minutes, add 4–8 mg, aiming for 8–16 mg on day 1 and 16 mg on day 2.

High-dose ("macro") induction — the Herring 2021 approach, a retrospective case series of 579 ED visits at Highland Hospital: escalate 4 mg → reassess 30–45 min → 8 mg → reassess → 16 mg, going higher in the same encounter if withdrawal persists. In that series >12 mg was given at 63.2% of visits and ≥28 mg at 23.8%, with no respiratory depression or sedation and no increase in precipitated withdrawal, and the approach extended withdrawal suppression after discharge — which matters enormously for a patient who may not make it to a follow-up appointment.

Extended-release buprenorphine before discharge is the option for the patient unlikely to follow up. ED-INNOVATION (JAMA 2026, N=1,994) found 7-day XR buprenorphine essentially equivalent to daily sublingual for 7-day engagement (40.5% vs 38.5%, not significant) with <1% precipitated withdrawal, plus lower craving and better satisfaction.

Every hour a hospitalized patient spends in withdrawal is an hour they are deciding whether to leave. Starting buprenorphine early is simultaneously the addiction treatment, the comfort measure, and the intervention that keeps them in the building long enough to finish their antibiotics.
2
Continue or start methadone
For patients already on it, or those buprenorphine cannot hold
▾
  • Already on OTP methadone? Verify the dose with the program by phone and document it before you give a milligram. Continuing home methadone during hospitalization is standard of care and is one of the most reliable ways to prevent a patient-directed discharge.
  • Inpatient initiation is permissible for a patient admitted for another condition — the "72-hour rule" allows up to three days of methadone for withdrawal while OTP linkage is arranged. Typical: 20–30 mg, with 5–10 mg additional for persistent withdrawal, then increases of 5–15 mg every 3–5 days.
  • Watch the QTc, and keep K⁺ ≥4.0 and Mg²⁺ ≥2.0.
3
Adjuncts — comfort care that does not treat the disease
Useful, necessary, and not a substitute for MOUD
▾
DrugDoseTarget symptomCautions
Clonidine0.1–0.3 mg PO q4–6h, titrated to BPAutonomic symptoms — sweating, anxiety, tachycardiaHold for SBP <90 or HR <50. Taper rather than stopping abruptly (rebound hypertension).
Lofexidine (Lucemyra)0.54 mg (three 0.18 mg tablets) PO four times daily, ~5–6 h apart, up to 14 days; taper over 2–4 daysSame α₂ mechanism as clonidine; the only FDA-approved non-opioid for opioid withdrawal (2018)Less hypotension than clonidine but still causes it; prolongs QT. Expensive — AAFP advises reserving it for patients not controlled by other agents.
Ondansetron4–8 mg PO/IV q8h PRNNausea and vomitingAdditive QT prolongation with methadone.
Loperamide2–4 mg PO, then 2 mg after each loose stool (max 16 mg/day)DiarrheaNever exceed the OTC maximum. Supratherapeutic loperamide is a sodium-channel blocker that causes torsades.
Hydroxyzine25–50 mg PO q6h PRNAnxiety, nausea, pruritusAnticholinergic burden; QT prolongation.
Dicyclomine20 mg PO q6h PRNAbdominal crampingAnticholinergic.
NSAIDs / acetaminophenStandard dosingMyalgia and bone painCheck renal function; avoid NSAIDs in AKI.
Trazodone50–100 mg PO at bedtimeInsomniaQT prolongation at higher doses.
Adjuncts are comfort care. They do not treat opioid use disorder. ASAM and CDC both state that withdrawal management without ongoing MOUD is not recommended and is associated with increased overdose death — because it strips tolerance without providing protection. Discharging a patient "detoxed" and unmedicated is more dangerous than not admitting them at all.
4
Precipitated withdrawal — treat it with MORE buprenorphine
Counterintuitive, and correct
▾

Recognize it: abrupt, severe withdrawal — COWS climbing toward 25+ — within 1–2 hours of the first buprenorphine dose in a patient who was previously comfortable. Fentanyl's redistribution out of adipose tissue makes this both more likely and less predictable than in the heroin era. But keep the fear proportionate: in D'Onofrio's multisite ED trial it occurred in 0.76% (9 of 1,200), and across 26 studies the reported range is 0–13.2%. It is a real complication you must know how to rescue — it is not a reason to withhold buprenorphine.

Precipitated withdrawal happens because buprenorphine's very high affinity displaces the full agonist, but its partial intrinsic activity does not replace the signal that was lost. The receptor goes from fully activated to partially activated in minutes. The fix follows directly from the mechanism: saturate the receptors with buprenorphine so that partial activation across all of them exceeds what the patient had. Giving less, or stopping, leaves them in the worst possible state.
  1. Escalating buprenorphine — 8 mg, then another 8–16 mg, up to a cumulative 24–32 mg.
  2. Adjuncts — clonidine, ondansetron, hydroxyzine or diphenhydramine, NSAIDs, loperamide, and benzodiazepines for agitation.
  3. Ketamine as a rescue agent — an NMDA antagonist that reduces withdrawal independently of μ binding, acting synergistically with buprenorphine. A pilot protocol using low-dose IM ketamine reported 98% of patients with a lower COWS at 30 minutes, 54% reaching minimal or no withdrawal, and median length of stay falling from 66 to 7 hours.
  4. Full agonist rescue (IV hydromorphone or fentanyl) is possible but blunted by buprenorphine's affinity, and risks re-entering the same cycle.
Prevention beats rescue. In a fentanyl-exposed patient, either wait for a higher COWS, or use low-dose ("Bernese") initiation with no washout, or use extended-release buprenorphine at a low COWS per ED-INNOVATION. And never abandon buprenorphine and discharge the patient in withdrawal — that is the exact sequence that ends in a fatal relapse.
5
α₂-agonist withdrawal — when nothing you try is working
Xylazine and, increasingly, medetomidine
▾
Xylazine and medetomidine are α₂-adrenergic agonists, not opioids. Chronic exposure downregulates central α₂ tone; abrupt cessation releases unopposed sympathetic outflow — the same physiology as clonidine rebound, but far more severe. The treatment therefore has to be replacement with an α₂ agonist, not opioids and not benzodiazepines.

The Philadelphia MMWR series of 165 patients defines the syndrome: median peak HR 145, SBP 195, DBP 122. It was resistant to opioids, benzodiazepines, clonidine, ketamine, olanzapine, ondansetron, and tizanidine. 83% responded to a dexmedetomidine infusion — conventional doses of 0.2–1.5 mcg/kg/hr, titrated to symptom control or to sedation for intubation (that is the range the series reported using, not a published ceiling) — which is an ICU intervention: 91% required ICU admission and 24% were intubated. Complications included posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and NSTEMI.

If your fentanyl-withdrawal patient is in autonomic crisis and escalating opioids and benzodiazepines are doing nothing, you are probably treating the wrong receptor. Call the ICU early — oral clonidine is frequently defeated by the vomiting, and this syndrome needs a titratable infusion.

Xylazine wound care

  • Treat the withdrawal and start MOUD first. Patients cannot tolerate wound care while in withdrawal, and patient-directed discharge is the main driver of treatment failure.
  • Distinguish an uninfected ulcer from cellulitis, abscess, and necrotizing infection — they are managed completely differently.
  • Do not reflexively debride. Many xylazine ulcers improve with moist wound care, compression, and reducing injection into the site.
  • Antibiotics only for documented infection; culture where possible.
  • Pre-medicate for wound care — it is exquisitely painful, and under-treating that pain is how you lose the patient.
  • Involve wound care, ID, surgery, addiction medicine, and social work together.
Monitor

What to trend every day

📈

The daily list

WhatWhy, and what a bad trend looks like
Respiratory rate + continuous EtCO₂The parameter that kills. A rising EtCO₂ with a falling rate is impending failure — act before the SpO₂ moves, because on oxygen it will move last.
SpO₂Useful, but understand it lags and is blunted by supplemental oxygen. Never the sole monitor.
RASSTarget 0 to −1. A drifting-down RASS in a patient on any opioid is the earliest behavioural sign of over-sedation.
COWSEvery 4–8 h during initiation, then daily. Rising COWS means your regimen is under-dosed — which is a flight risk as much as a comfort problem.
Heart rate and blood pressure trajectoryA climbing HR and SBP in a withdrawing patient who is not responding to opioids should make you think α₂-agonist withdrawal.
CKDaily until clearly falling if there was any down-time. Peaks at 24–72 h.
Creatinine, K⁺, Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻Rhabdomyolysis-driven AKI and hyperkalemia; hypocalcemia from calcium–phosphate precipitation.
ECG / QTcIf on methadone, on QT-prolonging combinations, or if loperamide overdose is suspected.
Wound examsDaily in anyone who injects — including sites they did not mention.
The discharge planEvery single day. The MOUD dose, the naloxone kit, and the follow-up appointment are clinical orders, not discharge paperwork.

When to call the ICU

⬆️

How to read these numbersThese are a practical escalation framework synthesized from the AHA 2023 poisoning update, ARDS guidelines, and standard critical care practice — not a single validated published rule. Use them as trigger points for a conversation with the ICU, not as a scoring system.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness, and the two things that must happen first

Ready for discharge when:

  • ≥6–12 h since the last naloxone with stable spontaneous ventilation — longer for long-acting agents
  • Ambulatory, oriented, tolerating oral intake
  • No hypoxemia off supplemental oxygen; chest film clear or improving
  • CK trending down, creatinine stable
  • Pain and withdrawal controlled on the planned outpatient regimen — not on IV medication
  • Psychiatric clearance if the overdose was intentional
Two things are non-negotiable before this patient leaves.

1. A take-home naloxone kit with education. The 2025 AHA Guidelines state that adults and children treated for opioid overdose should receive an opioid antagonist and instruction on how to use it at the time of discharge from a healthcare setting. Walley 2013 is the population evidence: a 46% reduction in overdose death rate.

2. A warm handoff to MOUD — a scheduled appointment or an actual dose given, not a phone number on a discharge sheet. D'Onofrio 2015: ED-initiated buprenorphine produced 78% engagement in treatment at 30 days versus 37% for referral alone and 45% for brief intervention, with illicit opioid use falling from 5.4 to 0.9 days/week. Larochelle 2018 showed the mortality benefit across 17,568 overdose survivors. A discharge without both of these is an incomplete discharge.

Home

Stable, ambulatory, has naloxone, has a confirmed MOUD appointment or an XR-buprenorphine dose on board. Ideally not alone for 24 h.

Home + OTP / office-based

Daily methadone at a certified opioid treatment program, or office-based buprenorphine — any DEA-registered Schedule III prescriber, no X-waiver required since the MAT Act.

Residential / inpatient rehab

Unstable housing, repeated failed outpatient attempts, or severe polysubstance use. Confirm the facility continues MOUD — many still do not, and abstinence-only placement raises overdose risk.

SNF

Needs 24 h skilled nursing — complex wound care, prolonged IV antibiotics for endocarditis or osteomyelitis — with less than 3 h/day of therapy.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Deficits from hypoxic-ischemic injury or critical illness myopathy, able to tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care such as ventilator weaning after severe anoxic injury or protracted ARDS.

Palliative / hospice

Devastating hypoxic-ischemic brain injury with a concordant multimodal prognosis — established at ≥72 h, never earlier.

Syringe services + peer support

Layer onto any of the above: sterile supplies, fentanyl and xylazine test strips, naloxone refills, and a peer recovery specialist.
🫀 ICU — airway, infusions, antidotes, and the sequelae that outlast the drug
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

  • Recurrent apnea, or any need for a naloxone infusion
  • Intubation for airway protection or ventilatory failure
  • Aspiration pneumonitis or pneumonia with hypoxemic respiratory failure
  • Opioid-associated noncardiogenic pulmonary edema requiring NIV or intubation
  • ARDS
  • Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury / post-cardiac-arrest care
  • Shock requiring vasopressors
  • Severe rhabdomyolysis with AKI, hyperkalemia, or need for renal replacement therapy
  • Compartment syndrome
  • Methadone-associated torsades or other malignant arrhythmia
  • Medetomidine or xylazine withdrawal needing a dexmedetomidine infusion — 91% of the Philadelphia cohort required ICU
  • Body packers with any sign of packet rupture
  • Any non-opioid toxidrome needing an antidote infusion — organophosphate, hyperthermic sympathomimetic, serotonin syndrome requiring paralysis, NMS
Airway

Intubation, ventilation & pulmonary edema

🌬️

The intubation decision

There is no validated rule here. The organising principle is that you intubate for failure to ventilate, not for a number — and specifically, you intubate when reversal is not going to be durable.

  • If naloxone plus bag-mask ventilation restores adequate spontaneous respiration, most patients do not need a tube.
  • GCS ≤8 is the conventional airway-protection threshold — but a purely opioid-obtunded patient who reverses cleanly is the classic exception.
  • EtCO₂ >60 mmHg and rising with inadequate respiratory effort supports intubation.
  • pH <7.20 with pCO₂ >60 in a patient not improving on naloxone → intubate.
  • Fentanyl chest-wall rigidity: if you cannot ventilate a patent airway, give a neuromuscular blocker — naloxone alone may fail.
  • Aspiration risk is high. Use rapid-sequence intubation with suction immediately available; many of these patients have a full stomach and absent airway reflexes.
Avoid succinylcholine after a prolonged down-time, crush injury, or established rhabdomyolysis — the potassium efflux can precipitate hyperkalemic cardiac arrest. Use rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg instead.
An intubated patient does not need naloxone. Once the airway is secured and ventilation is controlled, naloxone adds nothing and takes away a lot — precipitated withdrawal, agitation, a catecholamine surge, and a real risk of pulmonary edema. Secure the airway and let the drug wear off.
💧

Opioid-associated noncardiogenic pulmonary edema

Reported in roughly 0.2–10% of opioid overdoses — the wide range reflects genuinely different case definitions across series rather than uncertainty about the entity. Onset is typically within 4 hours, classically with pink frothy sputum.

Four non-exclusive mechanisms are proposed: increased pulmonary capillary permeability from hypoxia and histamine release (heroin is a potent histamine liberator); negative-pressure pulmonary edema from inspiratory effort against a closed glottis (laryngospasm or chest rigidity); a catecholamine surge — from hypoxia or from naloxone-precipitated withdrawal — causing pulmonary venoconstriction and a sharp rise in pulmonary artery pressure; and direct opioid-mediated lung injury. Importantly, this occurs in heroin overdose patients who never received naloxone, so it is not simply a naloxone complication.
DoDon't
Oxygen and CPAP/BiPAP — the mainstay. Refractory cases need invasive ventilation.Diuretics. The patient is euvolemic; this is a permeability and hemodynamic-transient problem, not volume overload. Furosemide wastes the intervention and risks hypotension and AKI.
PEEP — recruits and holds open flooded alveoli.Steroids. No role.
Echocardiogram if the picture is atypical or not resolving, to exclude a cardiogenic cause.Escalating naloxone — it does not treat the edema. Whether it causes it is much weaker than the teaching suggests: a 2024 systematic Naranjo-scored review of all 49 published cases graded 38 "possible" and 11 "probable" and none "definite," and in the classic series 74% of patients were already hypoxic on arrival. Withhold escalation because it is not helping, not because you have proven it caused this.
The prognosis is excellent and fast. In a retrospective series of 27 ED patients with heroin-induced noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, only about one-third needed mechanical ventilation and all but one were extubated at 24 hours. Radiographic and clinical resolution is typically 24–48 hours. This is a disease you support, not one you treat.
🫁

Aspiration, and ventilator settings if ARDS develops

Aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson)Aspiration pneumonia
CauseChemical injury from gastric acidBacterial infection
TimingImmediate — minutes to hours48–72 h after the aspiration event
FeverEarly, often transientPersistent or rising
CourseImproves with supportive care over 24–48 hProgresses without antibiotics
AntibioticsNo — early presumptive antibiotics select resistant organismsYes
The 48-hour rule. Roughly 20–25% of aspiration patients develop bacterial pneumonia at 48–72 h. Reassess at 48 hours: if symptoms have resolved, stop antibiotics; if there is no improvement and pneumonia is suspected, treat for 5–7 days. When treatment is indicated, follow the 2019 ATS/IDSA approach — ampicillin/sulbactam, a carbapenem, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Routine anaerobic coverage is no longer recommended for uncomplicated aspiration pneumonia; reserve it for lung abscess, empyema, or necrotizing pneumonia.
