Infusion

Naloxone infusion — the recipe

💉

Calculating and running it

The rule comes from Goldfrank's 1986 dosing nomogram (Ann Emerg Med) and is carried forward in the AHA 2023 antidote table: a continuous infusion of two-thirds of the bolus dose that produced reversal, each hour, maintains plasma naloxone at or above the level that would have existed 30 minutes after the bolus.

Enter the cumulative dose given until adequate spontaneous ventilation was achieved.
Infusion rate
0.27
mg/hour (⅔ of the waking dose)
  • Bridge the gap: give half the original bolus 15 minutes after starting the infusion, while it reaches steady state. (This step is a textbook refinement from Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies antidote monograph — it is not in the 1986 paper itself, which established only the two-thirds-per-hour rate.)
  • Titrate to respiratory rate ≥12 with adequate tidal volume and a normal EtCO₂ — not to alertness.
  • If the patient becomes agitated, diaphoretic, or vomiting → halve the infusion. Do not stop it abruptly; you will crash straight back into apnea.
  • Wean by 50% every 2–4 hours once the ingested agent's expected duration has elapsed, then observe for 2 hours after discontinuation before considering step-down.
  • A commonly quoted working range is 0.1–6 mg/hr.
Worked example: the patient reached adequate ventilation after a cumulative 0.12 mg. Run the infusion at 0.08 mg/hr, and give 0.06 mg (half the bolus) at 15 minutes. That is the entire calculation — and it is far more precise than the "just start 0.4 mg/hr" habit.
Antidotes

The other toxidromes — ICU management

🧪

Antidote doses — AHA 2023 Focused Update

These are the doses from the AHA's 2023 poisoning focused update, which remains the current antidote reference and was not superseded by the 2025 CPR guidelines.

AntidoteIndicationAdult initial doseMaintenance / titrationEndpoint & cautions
NaloxoneOpioids0.2–2 mg IV/IO/IM; 2–4 mg intranasalRepeat q2–3 min; infusion ⅔ of waking dose per hourTitrate to reversal of respiratory depression and return of protective airway reflexes — not arousal.
AtropineOrganophosphate / carbamate1–2 mg IV, DOUBLED every 5 minutesMaintenance 10–20% of the total loading dose per hour, up to 2 mg/hAHA 2023 states the endpoint verbatim: titrate to reversal of bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, and hypotension. Drying of pulmonary secretions is the endpoint that matters most — do not titrate to pupil size, which lags and may never normalize. Cumulative doses in the hundreds of milligrams may be required.
Atropineβ-blocker / CCB / digoxin bradycardia0.5–1.0 mg IV q3–5 minUp to 3 mg totalA holding measure while definitive therapy is prepared.
Pralidoxime (2-PAM)Organophosphate1–2 g IV loadInfusion 400–600 mg/h. WHO-referenced weight-based alternative: 30 mg/kg bolus then ≥8 mg/kg/hrReactivates acetylcholinesterase, addressing nicotinic effects. Evidence is contested — atropine is what saves the patient.
PhysostigmineAnticholinergic0.5–2 mg slow IV over ≥5 minRepeat q30–60 min as neededGet an ECG first. Withhold if there is ECG evidence of sodium-channel blockade — QRS >100 ms — or suspected TCA overdose, conduction disease, bradyarrhythmia, reactive airway disease, or bowel/bladder obstruction. Note the reappraisal: the "absolute" TCA contraindication traces to two 1980 case reports in which 2 mg was pushed over 3 minutes without bicarbonate; a 191-patient series found no asystole and a 1.0% seizure rate. The surviving rule is the ECG one, not a blanket ban. AHA 2023 does not address physostigmine, so no Class of Recommendation should be attributed to it.
FlumazenilBenzodiazepine0.2 mg IV, titrated up to 1 mgNo maintenance infusionUsually avoid — see the callout below.
Sodium bicarbonateSodium-channel blockade (TCA, loperamide, cocaine)50–150 mEq bolusInfusion: 150 mEq/L solution at 1–3 mL/kg/hMonitor for hypernatremia, alkalemia, hypokalemia. Titrate to QRS narrowing.
CyproheptadineSerotonin syndrome12 mg PO/NG onceThen 2 mg q2h until response; maintenance 4–8 mg q6h; max 32 mg/dayA 5-HT₂A antagonist; only available enterally. At 12–32 mg/24 h it binds 85–95% of serotonin receptors.
DantroleneNMS (severe)1–2.5 mg/kg IV q6–8hMax 10 mg/kg/day; transition to ~1 mg/kg PO q6h once stableDo not stop abruptly — rebound NMS is described; taper over ~10 days.
BromocriptineNMS2.5 mg PO/NG q8hTitrate to 5–10 mg q6–8h; max ~40 mg/dayRestores dopaminergic tone. Taper rather than stopping.
PhentolamineCocaine coronary vasospasm / hypertensive emergency1–2.5 mg IV q5–15 min PRNTitrate to blood pressure and symptomsOnly after adequate benzodiazepine sedation.
Lipid emulsion (20%)Local anesthetic systemic toxicity1.5 mL/kg, up to 100 mLThen 0.25 mL/kg/min for up to 30 minAll supporting studies used 20% emulsion.
High-dose insulinβ-blocker / CCB1 unit/kg bolusInfusion 1–10 units/kg/h with dextroseRegular human insulin. Monitor closely for hypoglycemia and hypokalemia.
Flumazenil in undifferentiated overdose. The AHA states that flumazenil "may cause harm in patients who are at increased risk for seizures or dysrhythmias, such as people who have seizure disorders, are dependent on benzodiazepines, or who have coingested other medications (such as tricyclic antidepressants). For this reason, the AHA does not recommend flumazenil administration in patients with undifferentiated drug overdose." A meta-analysis put the adverse-event risk ratio at 2.85 versus placebo and 3.81 for serious adverse events. In combined opioid-plus-benzodiazepine overdose, the AHA is explicit that naloxone, which has a better safety profile, should be given before flumazenil is even considered. Its legitimate niche is reversing iatrogenic over-sedation during procedural sedation in a patient with a known medication history and no benzodiazepine dependence.
🌡️

Serotonin syndrome — recognition and the hyperthermia trap

Diagnosis uses the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria (Dunkley & Isbister, QJM 2003), which are more sensitive and more specific than Sternbach's — 84% and 97% versus 75% and 96%.

Precondition: the patient must have taken a serotonergic agent. Serotonin toxicity is then present if any one of these is met:
  1. Spontaneous clonus
  2. Inducible clonus plus (agitation or diaphoresis)
  3. Ocular clonus plus (agitation or diaphoresis)
  4. Tremor plus hyperreflexia
  5. Hypertonia plus temperature >38 °C plus (ocular clonus or inducible clonus)
Run the interactive version on MDCalc. Note the whole rule is built around clonus — it is the single most specific finding, and it is worse in the lower limbs.

Treatment

  • Stop every serotonergic agent — the single most important step.
  • Benzodiazepines, titrated IV — first-line for agitation, tremor, autonomic instability, and hyperthermia, because they reduce the muscle activity generating the heat.
  • Cyproheptadine 12 mg once, then 2 mg q2h until response (max 32 mg/day).
  • Esmolol for autonomic hypertension and tachycardia — chosen because it is short-acting and reversible in a labile patient. Nitroprusside or nicardipine for hypertensive emergency.
  • Neuromuscular blockade and intubation for temperature >41.1 °C or refractory rigidity. Use a non-depolarizing agent — rocuronium or vecuronium, never succinylcholine given the rhabdomyolysis risk. Paralysis stops muscular heat production and is the definitive cooling intervention.
  • Active external cooling — ice packs, evaporative cooling, cooled IV fluids.
Antipyretics do not work here. Acetaminophen and NSAIDs lower a raised hypothalamic set point — but in serotonin syndrome and NMS the heat is generated by muscular activity, and the set point is normal. Giving them wastes time and provides false reassurance. Also avoid physical restraints without sedation: isometric contraction against restraints worsens both the hyperthermia and the rhabdomyolysis.
⚡

Sympathomimetic toxicity — sedate first

  • Per the AHA, "immediate treatment for life-threatening sympathomimetic poisoning is sedation to treat agitation." Escalating IV benzodiazepines are the mainstay — diazepam 5–10 mg IV q3–5 min, or lorazepam 2–4 mg IV, titrated to calm. Sedation treats the driver, and usually the tachycardia and hypertension resolve with it.
  • Hyperthermia: rapid external cooling. Immersion and evaporative cooling are more effective than cooling blankets, cold packs, or endovascular devices; for cocaine the AHA specifically recommends ice-water immersion.
  • Vasodilators — phentolamine and/or nitrates — for coronary vasospasm persisting after sedation, or for hypertensive emergency.
  • Sodium bicarbonate for cocaine-induced wide-complex tachycardia (cocaine behaves as a Vaughan-Williams class Ia/Ic agent); lidocaine is an alternative.
  • Refractory cardiogenic shock: intra-aortic balloon pump or VA-ECMO.
  • The AHA also notes that "the prolonged use of physical restraints without sedation is potentially harmful."
Haloperidol and typical antipsychotics are the wrong sedative in a hyperthermic sympathomimetic patient — they lower the seizure threshold, impair thermoregulation, prolong QT, and risk NMS. Benzodiazepines are the correct choice.
Beta-blockers in cocaine — an evolving questionThe classic teaching is that beta-blockade leaves "unopposed alpha" stimulation, worsening coronary vasospasm. The evidence base is weak and largely contradicts the theory — larger retrospective studies and meta-analyses suggest no harm from beta-blockers in patients with cocaine use, particularly for cocaine-associated chest pain or HFrEF. However, the 2014 ACC/AHA NSTE-ACS guideline still advises against beta-blockers in patients with signs of acute cocaine intoxication or possible vasospasm, and no subsequent guideline has formally rescinded it. The practical position: in the acutely intoxicated, hyperadrenergic patient, sedate with benzodiazepines — beta-blockade is neither necessary nor first-line. In a stable patient with remote cocaine use and a clear indication (HFrEF, post-MI), withholding a beta-blocker is likely the greater harm. Treat this as contested, not settled, in either direction.
Sequelae

The complications that outlast the drug

🩸

Rhabdomyolysis & compartment syndrome

ParameterNumber / action
DiagnosisCK >5× the upper limit of normal, or >1,000 IU/L. Many protocols use CK >5,000 U/L to trigger aggressive therapy.
FluidsIsotonic crystalloid (lactated Ringer's or 0.9% saline). A starting rate of ~400 mL/hr is commonly used, targeting urine output 1–3 mL/kg/hr — up to 200–300 mL/hr in crush-type injury — then titrated down over subsequent days.
DurationContinue IV fluids until CK <5,000 U/L and falling.
MonitorK⁺, Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻, creatinine, urine output, and compartments.
Bicarbonate / mannitolNot routinely recommended — the evidence does not show benefit over aggressive isotonic fluid alone.
Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis and a surgical emergency. The classic setting is a patient found down on a limb for hours. Suspect it with pain out of proportion, a tense compartment, and pain on passive stretch — paresthesia, pallor, and pulselessness are late findings. The number that decides it: delta pressure = diastolic BP − compartment pressure; <30 mmHg means fasciotomy. Do not wait for the CK, and do not wait for a pulse to disappear. Gluteal, thigh, and forearm compartments are the classic overdose sites.
🧠

Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury — and why not to prognosticate early

Multimodal neuroprognostication should be performed at ≥72 hours after return of spontaneous circulation — and later still if sedation is confounding — requiring concordant predictors across multiple domains. The ERC/ESICM framework predicts poor outcome when ≥2 of the following are present:

  • Absent pupillary AND corneal reflexes at ≥72 h
  • Bilaterally absent N20 SSEP at ≥24 h
  • Highly malignant EEG at >24 h
  • NSE >60 mcg/L at 72 h
  • Status myoclonus within 72 h
The overdose patient is a special case, and getting this wrong is lethal. Residual sedating drug is the dominant confounder — opioids, benzodiazepines, xylazine, medetomidine, and gabapentinoids all prolong apparent coma, and gabapentinoids accumulate further if there is AKI. Toxicologic causes of coma are, by their nature, potentially fully reversible. Establishing the cause of the arrest is critical precisely because etiology determines how reversible the injury is. Early withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy in an overdose patient is an error that looks defensible, is very hard to detect, and is impossible to undo. Give these patients time.
💓

QT, torsades, and the loperamide patient

Torsades de pointes arising from a prolonged QT. In this population the two names to think of are methadone (hERG blockade) and loperamide taken in massive doses — plus whatever QT-prolonging drugs have been stacked on top.
Jer5150, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons (Torsades de Pointes TdP.png)
A reminder of why ICU-level naloxone requirements have risen: the potency of what is in the supply has changed by orders of magnitude, while the antidote has not.
United States Drug Enforcement Administration, Public domain — Wikimedia Commons (Heroin Carfentanil Fentanyl Lethal Dose Close Up.jpg)

Methadone

Blocks hERG potassium channels. A systematic review found QTc prolongation in about 34% of maintenance patients with a pooled torsades incidence of 2%. QTc 450–500 ms → monitor more frequently and inform the patient; QTc >500 ms → decrease or discontinue. Torsades risk is highest above 500 ms or with an abrupt increase of >40 ms from baseline. RepIete K⁺ ≥4.0 and Mg²⁺ ≥2.0 — withdrawal-related vomiting and diarrhea deplete both, and the risk compounds.

Loperamide — "poor man's methadone"

At therapeutic doses (<16 mg/day) P-glycoprotein keeps loperamide out of the CNS. At 100–400 mg — with reports up to 1,200 mg/day — it saturates P-gp and crosses the blood–brain barrier for euphoria or withdrawal relief. The cardiotoxicity is not opioid at all: it is blockade of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels → QRS widening AND QTc prolongation → polymorphic VT, torsades, and sudden death. The FDA issued a safety communication in July 2016; a FAERS review identified 48 serious cardiac events including 13 cardiac arrests and 7 torsades.

Naloxone does not fix loperamide cardiotoxicity. Treat with sodium bicarbonate for the wide QRS and magnesium for torsades, with overdrive pacing or isoproterenol for refractory torsades and mechanical support (ECMO has been reported) in extremis. Ask about loperamide by name in any young patient with an unexplained wide-complex arrhythmia — they will not volunteer it, because they do not consider an anti-diarrheal a drug.
📦

Body packers vs body stuffers

Body packer ("mule")Body stuffer
IntentDeliberate traffickingPanicked ingestion to evade arrest
PackagingProfessionally wrapped — multiple layers of latex or polyethylene, often wax-coatedPoorly wrapped or unwrapped; baggie corners
NumberDozens to more than 100 packetsOne to a few
RiskCatastrophic toxicity if one ruptures; bowel obstruction and perforationEarly symptomatic toxicity, usually survivable
  • Asymptomatic packers: whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol electrolyte lavage solution at 1–2 L/hour orally or by NG tube until the rectal effluent is clear. PEG-ELS is isosmotic, is not absorbed, and does not cause fluid or electrolyte shifts.
  • Confirm clearance with repeat imaging — CT, because plain films miss packets — plus at least two to three packet-free stools.
  • Stuffers: activated charcoal if the airway is protected and within the window; observe 6–24 h depending on the drug.
  • Surgery for: symptomatic cocaine packers (sympathomimetic toxicity means presumed rupture), bowel obstruction or perforation, failure of packets to progress, or packets too large to pass. Once a packet ruptures, immediate removal of all packets is indicated.
Never perform gastric lavage on a body packer — it is unlikely to retrieve packets and may rupture them.
Opioid packers are the one group you can temporize — a naloxone infusion supports the patient while packets pass. Cocaine packers cannot be temporized, because there is no antidote. That single distinction drives the surgical decision.
Downgrade

When to step down

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Transfer to the ward when all of these are true:
  • ≥12–24 h off the naloxone infusion with RR ≥12 and stable EtCO₂ <45–50 mmHg
  • Extubated ≥6–12 h with stable gas exchange; SpO₂ ≥92% on ≤2–4 L nasal cannula
  • No vasopressors for ≥12–24 h
  • GCS ≥14, able to protect the airway; RASS −1 to 0
  • CK falling and <5,000 U/L; creatinine stable or improving; no renal replacement requirement
  • QTc <500 ms with no ectopy or arrhythmia for ≥24 h
  • Withdrawal controlled on an oral, ward-deliverable regimen — meaning off dexmedetomidine
  • Packets confirmed cleared, or the surgical problem resolved
Not yet if… the ingested agent's expected duration has not elapsed (methadone and extended-release products in particular); the patient still needs any naloxone; withdrawal requires an infusion the floor cannot run; the CK is still climbing; there is an unresolved compartment or wound question; or neuroprognostication is still pending. And do not downgrade a patient whose MOUD plan has not been started — the ICU stay is a captive opportunity to begin buprenorphine or methadone, and it is routinely wasted.

ICU-level disposition: most patients step down to the floor and follow the wards pathway. A minority with severe hypoxic-ischemic injury go to LTAC for ventilator weaning, to acute rehab if they can participate, or — only after concordant multimodal prognostication at ≥72 hours — to a palliative pathway.

Shared

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How each comorbidity changes the course and the management

ComorbidityHow it changes the diseaseHow it changes your management
Cirrhosis / hepatic impairment Reduced first-pass metabolism and prolonged half-lives mean standard doses accumulate. Sedation becomes a diagnostic trap — is this the opioid, or is this hepatic encephalopathy? Avoid morphine, codeine, and tramadol. Codeine is a CYP2D6-dependent prodrug, so analgesia fails while toxicity persists; sustained-release morphine has precipitated encephalopathy. Prefer fentanyl (start 25–50 mcg IV q1–2h and titrate) — its kinetics are largely unaffected by liver disease. Reduce and space hydromorphone (e.g. 0.2–0.4 mg IV q3–4h initially). The general rule is same dose, longer interval. For MOUD, the buprenorphine monoproduct is often preferred over the combination in advanced disease. Opioids directly antagonize lactulose by slowing transit — escalate the bowel regimen proactively and consider methylnaltrexone or naloxegol.
CKD / ESRD Renally cleared active metabolites accumulate, producing delayed and prolonged toxicity that looks like a second overdose hours later. Avoid morphine (M6G causes prolonged sedation; M3G is neuroexcitatory), codeine, and tramadol. Meperidine is contraindicated — normeperidine causes myoclonus and seizures and is not naloxone-reversible. Prefer fentanyl (no active metabolites), methadone (largely fecal excretion), and buprenorphine (no dose adjustment needed in renal impairment). Watch gabapentin and pregabalin — renally cleared, commonly overlooked, and a real cause of sedation and respiratory depression in dialysis patients; dosing may be as low as 100–300 mg after dialysis only. Naloxone itself is hepatically metabolized and needs no renal adjustment.
COPD / OSA / obesity hypoventilation Both produce exactly the physiology opioids attack — a blunted hypercapnic ventilatory drive and a collapsible upper airway. Overlap syndrome (COPD plus OSA) is the highest-risk phenotype, and postoperative opioid dosing in undiagnosed OSA is a recognized cause of in-hospital respiratory arrest. Screen with STOP-BANG before starting chronic opioids. Use the lowest effective MME, avoid benzodiazepine co-prescription absolutely, and offer naloxone. Any opioid escalation in a patient with known OSA who is not on PAP warrants continuous inpatient capnography.
Pregnancy Withdrawal is dangerous to the fetus, not just uncomfortable. Physiologic changes in the second and third trimesters increase methadone clearance. Methadone or buprenorphine is the standard of care (ACOG, SAMHSA, ASAM). Do not detox — tapering usually ends in relapse, and abrupt discontinuation "can result in preterm labor, fetal distress, or fetal demise." Methadone usually needs dose increases and often split BID dosing later in pregnancy. Do not initiate naltrexone; continuation in someone already stable on it is a shared decision. Give naloxone if she overdoses — maternal hypoxia is far more dangerous to the fetus than precipitated withdrawal — but use the lowest effective dose and monitor the fetus. NOWS is expected and treatable, never a reason to withhold MOUD: manage with rooming-in, swaddling, breastfeeding, and low stimulation first. Breastfeeding is encouraged on either medication.
Endocarditis / SSTI in people who inject Untreated OUD is the mechanism of readmission. 90-day readmission runs 22–49%, with about a third re-injecting by then. Fever plus injection use = blood cultures ×2 and an echocardiogram. Right-sided tricuspid S. aureus disease is classic, but left-sided disease is increasingly common. Treat the addiction and the infection simultaneously — retention on MOUD is associated with a 70% reduction in mortality in the month it is received. Addiction consultation increases antibiotic completion, decreases patient-directed discharge, and improves MOUD adherence. Discharging a patient with a PICC and no MOUD is a plan to readmit them. Partial oral antibiotic therapy is a reasonable option when a PICC is unsafe.
Psychiatric illness Depression, PTSD, anxiety, and ADHD are highly prevalent, and untreated illness drives relapse. A meaningful minority of overdoses are intentional. MOUD is not contraindicated by psychiatric illness and should not be withheld pending stabilization. Screen for suicidality. Watch QT-prolonging psychotropics stacked on methadone. On benzodiazepines: ASAM and SAMHSA are clear that benzodiazepine use is not an absolute contraindication to buprenorphine or methadone — the risk of untreated OUD exceeds the interaction risk. Manage, taper, and monitor; do not withhold treatment.
Chronic pain on long-term opioids A different population from OUD, though the two overlap. The dominant iatrogenic risk here is the forced taper. CDC 2022 explicitly warns against abrupt tapering or discontinuation — forced tapers are associated with overdose and suicide. Buprenorphine is increasingly used for chronic pain with problematic opioid use; low-dose initiation allows transition with no withdrawal window. Offer naloxone at ≥50 MME/day whether or not OUD is present.
Prolonged QTc / cardiac disease Methadone and high-dose loperamide are the two opioid-world causes of torsades; electrolyte losses from withdrawal compound them. Flag the stack: methadone plus ondansetron, haloperidol, droperidol, quetiapine, ziprasidone, citalopram or escitalopram, azithromycin or a respiratory fluoroquinolone, fluconazole or voriconazole, amiodarone or sotalol, hydroxyzine, loperamide. Keep K⁺ ≥4.0 and Mg²⁺ ≥2.0. If QTc becomes limiting, switch to buprenorphine rather than abandoning MOUD.
The drugs-to-avoid list — worth reading in full once.
Drug or combinationWhy
MeperidineNormeperidine accumulates → myoclonus and seizures, and it is not naloxone-reversible. Serotonin syndrome with MAOIs. There is essentially no remaining indication.
TramadolDose-dependent seizures (even at therapeutic doses), serotonin syndrome from its SNRI activity, unpredictable CYP2D6-dependent efficacy, hypoglycemia, and renal clearance. A weak analgesic with strong side effects.
Codeine in CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolizersExcessive conversion to morphine → fatal respiratory depression. Contraindicated in children post-tonsillectomy and in breastfeeding mothers (FDA boxed warning). Poor metabolizers get no analgesia at all.
Benzodiazepines + opioidsFDA boxed warning (2016) — profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. But note: this is a reason to avoid co-prescribing, not a reason to withhold MOUD from someone already taking benzodiazepines.
Flumazenil in chronic benzodiazepine use or undifferentiated overdoseWithdrawal seizures, and unmasking of co-ingested proconvulsants such as TCAs.
Physostigmine when TCA is suspected or QRS >100 msAsystole has been reported; it also lowers the seizure threshold. Get the ECG first.
Beta-blocker alone in acute cocaine intoxicationTheoretical unopposed alpha — the evidence is contested. Sedate first; do not withhold beta-blockade from a stable patient with a clear indication.
Haloperidol in hyperthermic sympathomimetic toxicityLowers the seizure threshold, impairs thermoregulation, prolongs QT, and risks NMS. Use benzodiazepines.
Succinylcholine after prolonged down-time or rhabdomyolysisHyperkalemic cardiac arrest. Use rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg.
Antipyretics for serotonin syndrome or NMS hyperthermiaIneffective — the heat is muscular, not hypothalamic.
Diuretics for opioid-associated noncardiogenic pulmonary edemaThe patient is not volume overloaded; risks hypotension and AKI.
Gastric lavage in body packersRisks packet rupture.
Loperamide above 16 mg/daySodium- and potassium-channel blockade → QRS widening, QT prolongation, and torsades.
Pearls

Practice-changing pearls

💡

The eighteen things that change what you actually do

  1. Titrate naloxone to breathing, not to consciousness. In a dependent patient start at 0.04–0.05 mg IV and repeat every 1–2 minutes until they are ventilating adequately. The target is RR ≥12 with a normal EtCO₂ — not an awake, angry, vomiting patient. Over-reversal buys agitation, aspiration, a catecholamine surge, and pulmonary edema.
  2. Naloxone pauses the overdose; it does not treat it. Naloxone's half-life is 30–80 minutes; methadone's reaches 59 hours. Every reversed patient is a countdown clock, and the observation period is dictated by the agent's kinetics, not naloxone's.
  3. Fentanyl chest-wall rigidity is a ventilation problem naloxone may not fix. If you cannot bag-mask a patent airway after an opioid exposure, think "wooden chest" and give a neuromuscular blocker.
  4. Learn the α₂-agonist non-response pattern. Naloxone given → respirations improve → patient stays deeply sedated and bradycardic. That is not naloxone failure and not a reason to keep pushing. Support the airway and wait.
  5. Medetomidine withdrawal is an ICU disease. Median peak HR 145 and SBP 195; 91% needed ICU and 24% were intubated. It resists opioids, benzodiazepines, clonidine, ketamine, olanzapine, and tizanidine — and 83% responded to dexmedetomidine at conventional doses of 0.2–1.5 mcg/kg/hr. If nothing is working, you are treating the wrong receptor.
  6. EtCO₂ beats SpO₂, especially on supplemental oxygen. Oximetry measures oxygenation and lags 2–3 minutes; capnography measures ventilation. Respiratory depression was ~17.6× more likely to be detected by capnography in procedural-sedation studies. Oxygen without capnography blinds your own monitor.
  7. Fentanyl does not appear on a standard urine opiate immunoassay. The assay targets morphine-class compounds; fentanyl is a phenylpiperidine with minimal cross-reactivity. A negative opiate screen means nothing. Order a fentanyl-specific assay — and know that methadone, buprenorphine, oxycodone, and the nitazenes each need their own.
  8. Buprenorphine's ceiling is why it is safe — and why its overdoses resist reversal. Low intrinsic activity plateaus respiratory depression, but very high affinity and slow dissociation mean buprenorphine-associated respiratory depression is relatively resistant to naloxone even at high doses. Plan for an infusion and prolonged support, not a single push.
  9. Treat precipitated withdrawal with more buprenorphine. Escalate to a cumulative 24–32 mg, add adjuncts, and consider ketamine as rescue (one protocol dropped median length of stay from 66 hours to 7). Never send the patient out in withdrawal — that is the sequence that ends in a fatal relapse.
  10. Methadone kills on days 3–10, not day 1. Analgesia lasts 6–8 hours while the half-life reaches 59 — patients feel under-dosed as drug accumulates, and die at home during sleep. Fatal toxicity risk in the first two weeks has been estimated at 6.7× that of untreated heroin users. Titrate 5–15 mg every 3–5 days and warn every patient about the first fortnight.
  11. Loperamide is "poor man's methadone" and a sodium-channel blocker. At 100–400 mg it saturates P-glycoprotein and enters the CNS; the cardiotoxicity is QRS widening plus QT prolongation → torsades. Naloxone does not fix it — use bicarbonate for the wide QRS and magnesium for torsades. Ask about it by name.
  12. Plain abdominal films miss packets — CT is the study. Confirm clearance with CT plus documented packet-free stools, not a single KUB. And never lavage a packer.
  13. Hypoglycemia is the great mimic, and opioids can cause it. Check a glucose on every altered patient and check it again. Tramadol is the classic culprit. A missed hypoglycemia looks exactly like a naloxone-refractory overdose.
  14. The gabapentinoid co-ingestion trend is real and under-recognized. CDC found gabapentin in 9.7% of overdose deaths across 23 states, judged contributory in about half of those. The FDA issued a respiratory-depression warning in December 2019. Gabapentinoids are renally cleared — in a CKD patient on opioids this is a slow-motion respiratory arrest. Ask by name; patients do not consider them drugs.
  15. Do not prognosticate the overdose patient's brain before 72 hours — and preferably later. Residual drug is the dominant confounder and toxicologic coma is potentially fully reversible. Early withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy here is an error that is very hard to detect and impossible to undo.
  16. Diuretics do not treat opioid-associated noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Oxygen, CPAP/BiPAP, and PEEP. Expect resolution in 24–48 hours — in one series all but one patient were extubated at 24 hours.
  17. Anticholinergic is dry and hot; cholinergic is wet everywhere. The fastest bedside discriminator is the axilla. And in cholinergic poisoning, titrate atropine to dry lungs, not to heart rate or pupil size — the killer B's are what kill, and doses in the hundreds of milligrams may be needed.
  18. Everyone who survives an overdose leaves with naloxone and a MOUD plan. The 2025 AHA guidelines make discharge naloxone explicit. D'Onofrio 2015 (78% vs 37% engagement) and Larochelle 2018 (mortality reduction) make the MOUD handoff a mortality intervention, not a social nicety. A discharge without both is an incomplete discharge.

A note on sourcingAntidote doses in this guide are taken from the AHA 2023 poisoning focused update wherever it covers the agent, because it is the most recent document that assigns a Class of Recommendation to antidote therapy. Where a number comes from somewhere else — a drug label, a single trial, or a case series — that source is named in the table cell itself. The ICU escalation and downgrade thresholds are practice consensus, synthesized from the AHA update, ARDS guidance, and standard critical care practice; they are not a published, validated rule, and they are labelled as such where they appear.

Rule plus clinician judgment still missed ~1.9% (10 of 529). The St. Paul's derivation (Christenson 2000, n=573, sens 99% / spec 40%) specifies SpO₂ >92% on room air; secondary summaries that quote >95% for it are wrong. Sources disagree on whether HOUR kept 92% or deliberately raised it to 95% — 92% is the defensible number to teachJustifies a one-hour observation for carefully selected patients — and quantifies exactly how it fails. Acad Emerg Med 2019;26:7
Herring — high-dose ED buprenorphine2021Retrospective case series (not a trial), 579 visits / 391 patients, Highland Hospital>12 mg given in 63.2% of visits and ≥28 mg in 23.8%, with no respiratory depression or sedation and no increase in precipitated withdrawalUnderwrites the high-dose initiation strategy used when fentanyl makes conventional dosing inadequate. JAMA Netw Open 2021;4:e2117128
ED-INNOVATION (D'Onofrio, CTN-0099)2026Multisite RCT, N=1,994 (991 extended-release vs 1,003 sublingual buprenorphine)Engagement at 7 days 40.5% vs 38.5% (difference 1.6%, 95% CI −2.8 to 6.0 — not significant); precipitated withdrawal 0.6% vs 0.8% with enrollment at COWS ≥4 and 76% fentanyl positivityThe best evidence that initiating in the COWS 4–7 range is safer than fentanyl-era fear suggested. Note 4 was the eligibility threshold — the 8-point threshold still governed in-ED dosing, so this is not a licence to dose at 4. JAMA 2026;335(11):948–960 (erratum 335(16):1452)
Goldfrank — naloxone infusion nomogram1986Pharmacokinetic modelling studyInfusing two-thirds of the effective bolus per hour maintains plasma naloxone at or above the concentration present 30 minutes after that bolusThe origin of the infusion recipe in the ICU panel, still carried in the AHA 2023 antidote table. Ann Emerg Med 1986;15:566
Kelly AM — intranasal vs intramuscular naloxone2005Prehospital RCT, N=155, 2 mg per armIM was superior: 82% vs 63% achieved >10 spontaneous respirations/min within 8 minutes (P=0.017), using the old dilute intranasal formulationRoute matters — but this result was superseded by Kerr 2009 (n=172), which found concentrated intranasal naloxone equivalent to IM (72.3% vs 77.5%, NS). Together they are why modern 4 mg concentrated devices exist. Med J Aust 2005;182:24
Dunkley/Isbister — Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria2003Derivation and validation, Hunter Area Toxicology ServiceSensitivity 84%, specificity 97% — against Sternbach criteria at 75%/96%The decision rule used in the ICU panel to separate serotonin toxicity from NMS. QJM 2003;96:635
Wesson & Ling — COWS2003Expert-derived 11-item scale; later concurrent validation against naloxone challenge (Tompkins 2009)Maximum 48 points; bands 5–12 mild, 13–24 moderate, 25–36 moderately severe, >36 severeThe scale reimplemented in the clinic calculator on this page. J Psychoactive Drugs 2003;35:253
MMWR — medetomidine withdrawal, Philadelphia2025Case series (Huo S et al.), N=165, Sept 2024 – Jan 2025Median peak HR 145, SBP 195, DBP 122. 91% required ICU, 24% were intubated, 83% responded to dexmedetomidine (0.2–1.5 mcg/kg/hr, titrated). Resistant to opioids, benzodiazepines, clonidine, ketamine, olanzapine and tizanidineThe clinical description of the adulterant that has displaced xylazine in some markets. Cite these figures to the MMWR — the same group's later, larger cohort (London KS et al., J Addict Med 2026;20:231, N=209) reports different numbers (77.5% ICU, 20.1% intubated). MMWR 2025
HEALing Communities Study2024Cluster-randomized trial across 67 communities in 4 states — the largest addiction-prevention trial ever runNull. The community-engaged intervention did not significantly reduce opioid overdose deaths (adjusted rate ratio 0.91, not significant)A necessary corrective to optimism: bundling evidence-based practices at community scale, during the fentanyl surge, did not measurably move mortality. Individual-level treatment still works; population-level implementation is harder than it looks. NEJM 2024
Payne — 8 mg vs 4 mg intranasal naloxone2024Observational comparison, New York law-enforcement administration, Mar 2022 – Aug 2023No difference in survival or number of doses needed, but the 8 mg product carried 2.51× the risk of withdrawal signs including vomiting (95% CI 1.51–4.18)The evidence against reflexively reaching for the highest-milligram device. Every current nasal-spray label now warns that comparing products "on a nominal mg-for-mg basis may be misleading." MMWR 2024;73:110
ARDSNet / ARMA2000RCT, N=861, 6 vs 12 mL/kg predicted body weightMortality 31% vs 40%; ventilator-free days 12 vs 10The basis for the lung-protective settings used if overdose-associated ARDS develops. NEJM 2000;342:1301
Also worth knowingMOTHER (buprenorphine vs methadone in pregnancy — milder neonatal opioid withdrawal with buprenorphine, comparable maternal outcomes) · POATS (prescription-opioid OUD; success required ongoing buprenorphine, with relapse on taper) · EXHIT ENTRE / CTN-0098 (extended-release buprenorphine started in hospitalized patients) · SALOME / NAOMI (injectable diacetylmorphine and hydromorphone for refractory OUD — Canadian, not applicable to US practice).

Scores — calculators on this page vs deliberately linked out

ScoreHere?Why
COWSLive calculator (Clinic)All 11 items and point values are published openly by NIDA and verifiable — safe to reimplement.
St. Paul's / HOUR ruleLive checklist (Wards)Six explicit criteria, fully specified in the validation paper.
Naloxone infusionLive calculator (ICU)Arithmetic from a published nomogram, not a risk score.
Hunter Serotonin Toxicity CriteriaLinked outThe seven clinical features and the 84%/97% performance are verified, but the exact branching text could not be re-verified from open-access full text — so the branches are presented as teaching content and the calculator is MDCalc's.
Poisoning Severity ScoreLinked outIPCS/EAPCCT grading is organ-system-based and narrative, not an additive point score — it cannot be honestly reimplemented as one.
SAD PERSONSDeliberately omittedPoor predictive performance; not recommended for suicide risk stratification. Use a structured assessment such as the C-SSRS.
